examples: 4-digit numbers formed from {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}: First digit cannot be 0 (4 choices)
Even numbers: Last digit must be even

types.name: 4. Circular Arrangements & Necklaces
types.desc: Arranging people around round tables or stringing distinct colored beads onto necklaces.
examples: Seating 6 people at a round dining table = (6 - 1)! = 5! = 120 ways
Necklace of 6 distinct gemstones = (6 - 1)! / 2 = 60 ways

types.name: 5. Gap and Tie (String) Methods
types.desc: Tie method keeps items strictly together; Gap method ensures no two specified items are adjacent.
examples: Tie method: Bundle items together into 1 super-item, multiply by internal permutations
Gap method: Place other items first, then arrange restricted items in created gaps

rules.title: Permutation vs Combination Core Test
rules.explanation:
- **Permutation ($P$)**: Order matters (e.g., telephone numbers, ranking, anagrams, officer posts like President/VP).
- **Combination ($C$)**: Order does NOT matter (e.g., handshakes, committee members, team selection, picking balls from urns).
Formula bridge: ${}^n P_r = r! \times {}^n C_r$.
rules.correct: Selecting a team of 4 from 10: Order does not matter, use 10C4 = 210.
rules.incorrect: Using 10P4 which counts different orderings of the exact same 4 teammates as separate teams.

rules.title: String / Tie Method for 'Always Together'
rules.explanation:
When $k$ particular objects must always be together:
(1) Tie them together into a single composite unit.
(2) The total number of items to arrange is $(n - k + 1)$.
(3) Multiply the arrangement of the composite units by the internal arrangements of the tied items: $(n - k + 1)! \times k!$.
rules.correct: Arranging 5 boys and 2 girls so girls are together: Treat 2 girls as 1 unit. Total units = 5 + 1 = 6. Total = 6! * 2! = 720 * 2 = 1440.
rules.incorrect: Calculating 7! and subtracting 2!.

rules.title: Gap Method for 'No Two Adjacent / Never Together'
rules.explanation:
When specific objects must NEVER be adjacent:
(1) Arrange the unrestricted objects first in $m!$ ways, creating $(m + 1)$ gaps (including ends).
(2) Place the $k$ restricted objects into the available $(m + 1)$ gaps using ${}^{m+1} P_k$ or ${}^{m+1} C_k \times k!$.
rules.correct: Arrange 4 boys and 3 girls so no two girls are adjacent: 4 boys seated in 4! = 24 ways, creating 5 gaps. 3 girls placed in 5 gaps in 5P3 = 60 ways. Total = 24 * 60 = 1440.
rules.incorrect: Calculating Total - (Girls together) which only subtracts all 3 together, leaving cases where 2 girls are together.

rules.title: Circular Permutation Clockwise/Anticlockwise Symmetry
rules.explanation:
- For people around a round table where clockwise and anticlockwise orderings are distinct: $(n - 1)!$.
- For garlands, necklaces, or key rings where flipping over makes clockwise and anticlockwise identical: $\frac{(n - 1)!}{2}$.
rules.correct: Number of ways to string 5 different beads on a necklace = (5 - 1)! / 2 = 4! / 2 = 24 / 2 = 12.

rules.title: Repeated Elements Anagram Rule
rules.explanation: If a collection of $n$ items contains $p$ identical items of type 1, $q$ of type 2, and $r$ of type 3, the number of distinct permutations is $\frac{n!}{p! \cdot q! \cdot r!}$.
rules.correct: Letters of 'MISSISSIPPI' (11 letters: 1 M, 4 I, 4 S, 2 P) = 11! / (4! * 4! * 2!) = 34,650.
rules.incorrect: Calculating 11! without dividing by duplicate factorials.

rules.title: Handshake / Line Segment Formula
rules.explanation: When $n$ people shake hands with each other once, or when connecting $n$ non-collinear points to form straight line segments, the total number is ${}^n C_2 = \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}$.
rules.correct: At a conference of 12 people, total handshakes = 12 * 11 / 2 = 66.
rules.incorrect: Multiplying 12 * 11 = 132 (double counting every handshake).

common_mistakes.mistake: Using permutations (nPr) when forming a committee or selecting players.
common_mistakes.correction: Use combinations (nCr) because changing the order of people chosen does not create a new committee.
common_mistakes.rationale: A committee of Alice and Bob is identical to a committee of Bob and Alice.

common_mistakes.mistake: Solving 'no two girls together' by subtracting 'all girls together' from total.
common_mistakes.correction: Use the Gap Method. Total minus (all together) still includes cases where exactly two girls sit together.
common_mistakes.rationale: Complement of 'no two together' is 'at least two together', not 'all together'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that zero cannot occupy the first digit in multi-digit number problems.
common_mistakes.correction: The leading most significant digit has only (n - 1) options if 0 is an available digit.
common_mistakes.rationale: A number starting with 0 (e.g., 0452) reduces to a 3-digit number.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to divide by 2 for circular necklaces or garlands.
common_mistakes.correction: Dividing by 2 is essential because a necklace can be flipped over, making clockwise and anticlockwise identical.
common_mistakes.rationale: Rotational 3D reflection invariance.

quick_revision_points: Order matters => Permutations: nPr = n! / (n - r)!
Order does NOT matter => Combinations: nCr = n! / [r!(n - r)!]
nCr = nC(n-r); nC0 = 1; nCn = 1; nC1 = n
Handshake / line segments = nC2 = n(n - 1) / 2
Anagram with repeats = n! / (p! * q! * r!)
Round table seating = (n - 1)!; Necklace/garland = (n - 1)! / 2
'Always together' => Tie method: treat as 1 unit
'Never together' => Gap method: seat others first, then place in gaps

lessons.title: Analogy: Word, Numerical, Alphabetical & Dual-Relation Logic

content_json.definition: Analogy is a cognitive reasoning process that evaluates the correspondence or relational equivalence between two distinct entities or pairs of elements. In competitive exams (SSC CGL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC, IBPS PO, State PSCs), analogy tests semantic links (worker-tool, cause-effect, antonym-synonym, animal-habitat), mathematical transformations (square/cube shifts, prime clusters, digit operations), and positional letter variations.
content_json.overview:
Fundamental Analogy Relationships:
- Semantic / Word Analogy: Worker & Tool (Carpenter : Saw), Quantity & Unit (Current : Ampere), Country & Capital/Currency (Japan : Yen)
- Number Analogy: Operations of the form $x : x^2 \pm k$, $x : x^3 \pm k$, $x : (x \times k) + c$, sum of digits, or prime number sequencing
- Alphabet Analogy: Positional shifts (Forward $+n$, Backward $-n$), reverse pairs ($A \leftrightarrow Z, B \leftrightarrow Y$), sum of letter ranks
- Double Analogy: Finding simultaneous dual pairs conforming to an identical underlying governing pattern ($A : B :: C : D$)

types.name: 1. Semantic & Verbal Knowledge Analogy
types.desc: Relationships based on vocabulary, science, geography, instruments, and social conventions.
examples: Barometer : Pressure :: Hygrometer : Humidity
Ornithologist : Birds :: Paleontologist : Fossils

types.name: 2. Numerical & Mathematical Operation Analogy
types.desc: Mathematical transformations linking numbers through powers, products, or arithmetic operations.
examples: 12 : 144 :: 14 : 196 (Direct perfect squares)

types.name: 3. Alphabetical & Letter-Shift Analogy
types.desc: Positional changes in alphabetical ranking, reverse symmetry, or skipped steps.
examples: LOCK : MPDL :: READ : SFBE (+1 forward shift to each character)
AZ : BY :: CX : DW (Opposite letter pairs)

types.name: 4. Mixed / Alpha-Numeric Analogy
types.desc: Interlocking relationships between letters and their positional numeric values or sums.

types.name: 5. Group / Set Analogy
types.desc: Selecting an option triplet that shares the exact relational rule found in a given set of numbers.
examples: Given set (7, 13, 20): 7 + 6 = 13, 13 + 7 = 20 (Differences increment by 1)
Given set (4, 16, 64): Powers of 4 (4^1, 4^2, 4^3)

rules.title: Prime Number Priority Rule in Numerical Analogies
rules.explanation:
When evaluating number analogies, hierarchy of operations must be applied:
1. Prime number sequence
2. Square and Cube operations
3. Multiplication and Division
4. Addition and Subtraction
If a relationship can be explained by both prime numbers and arithmetic addition, the prime rule takes precedence.
rules.correct: 4 : 9 :: 25 : 49 (Squares of consecutive primes: 2^2, 3^2, 5^2, 7^2).
rules.incorrect: Selecting 36 because 4 to 9 is +5 and 25 + 11 = 36.

rules.title: Directional Order of Analogy Rule
rules.explanation: The relationship must be maintained strictly in the original order ($A \rightarrow B$ must correspond to $C \rightarrow D$). Reversing the subject and object or tool and worker produces a false analogy.
rules.correct: Author : Novel :: Sculptor : Statue (Creator followed by Creation).
rules.incorrect: Author : Novel :: Statue : Sculptor (Inverted order).

rules.title: Opposite Letter Sum of 27 Rule
rules.explanation: Two letters are reverse counterparts in the 26-letter English alphabet if and only if the sum of their positional values equals 27: Rank(A) + Rank(Z) = 1 + 26 = 27; Rank(M) + Rank(N) = 13 + 14 = 27.
rules.correct: H (rank 8) corresponds to S (rank 19) because 8 + 19 = 27.
rules.incorrect: Pairing H with T (sum = 28).

rules.title: Digit Sum & Product Rule
rules.explanation: In number analogies with large multi-digit integers where algebraic transformations fail, check the digital root (sum of digits) or product of digits.
rules.incorrect: Attempting complex polynomial division on multi-digit numbers.

rules.title: Grammatical Part-of-Speech Invariance Rule
rules.explanation: If the first word pair connects two adjectives, the answer pair must also consist of two adjectives. An adjective cannot form a valid analogy with a noun or adverb if an adjective option exists.
rules.correct: Courageous : Brave (Adjectives) :: Rapid : Swift (Adjectives).
rules.incorrect: Courageous : Brave :: Rapid : Quickness (Pairing an adjective with a noun).

common_mistakes.mistake: Reversing the relation order between the first and second pairs.
common_mistakes.correction: Always verify that if Pair 1 is (Cause : Effect), Pair 2 must strictly be (Cause : Effect).
common_mistakes.rationale: Exam traps intentionally place the inverted relationship (Effect : Cause) as Option A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying simple addition instead of checking for square or prime relations.
common_mistakes.correction: Always test powers ($n^2 \pm k, n^3 \pm k$) and prime sequences before settling for simple addition.
common_mistakes.rationale: Exam answer keys follow the standard priority: Prime > Square/Cube > Product > Addition.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming only forward alphabetical letter counting.
common_mistakes.correction: Remember circular wrapping ($Z \rightarrow A$) and backward reverse pairing ($A \leftrightarrow Z$).
common_mistakes.rationale: Letters often wrap backwards (e.g. B - 3 = Y).

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring the specific context of multiple-meaning words.
common_mistakes.correction: Determine the exact technical or semantic domain of the first pair before evaluating options.
common_mistakes.rationale: Words like 'Current', 'Bank', or 'Cell' have completely distinct scientific vs economic contexts.

quick_revision_points: Hierarchy of Number Logic: Prime Numbers > Squares/Cubes > Multiply/Divide > Add/Subtract
Opposite letters always sum to 27: A(1)+Z(26)=27, B(2)+Y(25)=27, C(3)+X(24)=27
EJOTY rule gives benchmarks: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25
Common patterns: n^2 + 1, n^2 - 1, n^3 + n, n^3 - n, (n * (n+1))
Word analogies require strict identity of grammatical category and order
When operations on large integers seem arbitrary, check sum or product of digits

lessons.title: Classification: Odd One Out in Semantic, Numerical & Letter Groups

content_json.definition: Classification (Odd One Out) requires isolating an anomalous element from a set of four or five entities where all remaining items share a specific, well-defined common attribute, taxonomic class, or mathematical rule. Tested across SSC CGL, Bank PO, Railways, and Defense exams, classification problems evaluate semantic taxonomy (mammals vs reptiles, metals vs non-metals), arithmetic grouping (prime numbers, squares/cubes, parity), and letter cluster patterns (vowel counts, rank intervals).
content_json.overview:
Fundamental Classification Categories:
- Word / Semantic Classification: Common biological kingdom, geographical landform (peninsula vs island), state capitals, SI units
- Numerical Classification: Divisibility rules, prime vs composite numbers, cubes and squares, sum of digits
- Alphabetical / Letter Classification: Vowel-consonant composition, step differences between consecutive letters (+2, +3), reverse opposite pairs
- Paired Classification: Pairs of numbers or words sharing a fixed operational ratio ($x : 3x + 1$) where one pair deviates

types.name: 1. Word & Semantic Classification
types.desc: Identifying the odd word based on biological, scientific, historical, or linguistic taxonomy.
examples: Whale, Dolphin, Bat, Shark (Shark is the odd one out; it is a fish, while the others are mammals)
Paris, Berlin, Rome, New York (New York is the odd one; the others are national capitals)

types.name: 2. Numerical Property Classification
types.desc: Finding the odd number using prime properties, divisibility, or powers.
examples: 23, 29, 31, 35 (35 is odd one out; it is composite, others are prime numbers)
27, 64, 125, 144 (144 is the odd one; it is a square, while the others are cubes: 3^3, 4^3, 5^3)

types.name: 3. Letter Cluster & Alphabetical Shift
types.desc: Analyzing positional intervals between letters within four-letter clusters.
examples: BDF, HJL, PRT, KMO (All have +2 step intervals; if an option has +2, +3 it is the odd one)
AEI, IOU, EIO, BCD (BCD is the odd one; it has no vowels, while others consist entirely of vowels)

types.name: 4. Number Pair / Group Classification
types.desc: Evaluating mathematical operations linking pairs of numbers to detect the inconsistent pair.

types.name: 5. Geometrical & Symbol Classification
types.desc: Sorting by geometric attributes: lines of symmetry, number of sides, closed vs open curves.
examples: Triangle, Square, Pentagon, Circle (Circle is the odd one; it has no straight edges/vertices)

rules.title: Prime vs Composite Superiority Rule
rules.explanation: In number classification, the property of being a prime number takes precedence over odd/even parity and simple divisibility rules.
rules.correct: In {13, 17, 23, 27}, 27 is the odd one out because it is composite (3^3), while 13, 17, 23 are primes.
rules.incorrect: Selecting 13 claiming it has the lowest value.

rules.title: Universal Group Property Verification Rule
rules.explanation: To validate that element $X$ is the odd one out, you must establish a specific positive property shared by ALL remaining elements, not merely an arbitrary uniqueness of $X$.
rules.correct: In {Copper, Silver, Gold, Coal}, Coal is the odd one out because Copper, Silver, and Gold are all metals.
rules.incorrect: Selecting Silver because 'it begins with S' (superficial attribute).

rules.title: Letter Cluster Step-Interval Verification
rules.explanation: Write numerical ranks for each letter in the cluster and calculate forward differences. The odd cluster will have a different step sequence.
rules.incorrect: Guessing by visual appearance of letters.

rules.title: Digit Sum Rule for Large Integers
rules.explanation: When 4-digit or 5-digit numbers are presented without clear power relations, calculate the sum of digits. In three options, the sum will be identical (or follow a rule like even sum), while the fourth deviates.
rules.incorrect: Attempting multi-digit prime factorization in a 60-second exam.

rules.title: Taxonomic Biological Hierarchy Rule
rules.explanation: In biology-based classification, always classify at the highest appropriate scientific taxon (e.g., Mammals vs Birds/Reptiles/Amphibians/Pisces, Warm-blooded vs Cold-blooded).
rules.correct: {Bat, Whale, Elephant, Ostrich}: Ostrich is the odd one out because it is an Aves (bird), whereas Bat, Whale, and Elephant are all mammals.
rules.incorrect: Selecting Whale because 'it lives in the water' (ignoring that both bats and whales are warm-blooded mammals).

common_mistakes.mistake: Picking an option simply because 'it looks different' without proving the other three share a common rule.
common_mistakes.correction: Always define the shared attribute of the other three options first before confirming the odd one.
common_mistakes.rationale: Exam questions often contain distractor options with superficial differences.

common_mistakes.mistake: Classifying whale or dolphin as fish.
common_mistakes.correction: Whales, dolphins, and porpoises are marine mammals (give live birth, breathe with lungs).
common_mistakes.rationale: High-frequency trap in SSC CGL and RRB general mental ability tests.

common_mistakes.mistake: Focusing on odd/even parity while ignoring that one number is a prime or perfect square.
common_mistakes.correction: Test for perfect squares, cubes, and prime numbers before checking even/odd parity.
common_mistakes.rationale: Parity is the lowest priority rule in competitive classification problems.

common_mistakes.mistake: Ignoring circular wrapping in letter series (+2 from Y reaches A).
common_mistakes.correction: Count letters modularly: Z+1 = A, Z+2 = B.
common_mistakes.rationale: Clusters like XZA follow a regular +2, +1 pattern.

quick_revision_points: Hierarchy of Number Classification: Prime Numbers > Powers (Cubes/Squares) > Multiples/Divisibility > Digital Sum > Parity
Whale, Dolphin, Bat, Platypus are MAMMALS (not fish or birds)
Letter clusters: Convert immediately to numbers (A=1 ... Z=26) and check differences
Opposite letter pairs sum to 27: AZ, BY, CX, DW, EV, FU, GT, HS, IR, JQ, KP, LO, MN
In number pairs (a, b), test if b = a^2, b = a^3, b = 2a + 1, or b = a * (a+1)
Never select an answer without verifying the positive rule uniting the remaining three

lessons.title: Number Series: Arithmetic, Geometric, Two-Tier Differences & Polynomial Sequences

content_json.definition: A Number Series is an ordered sequence of numbers governed by a deterministic logical, arithmetic, or polynomial recurrence relation. Competitive exams (IBPS PO, SBI PO, SSC CGL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC, CAT) test candidates on detecting common differences ($d$), common ratios ($r$), two-tier differences ($\Delta_1, \Delta_2$), alternating interlocked sequences, fibonacci additions, and combinations of powers with linear shifts ($n^2 \pm k, n^3 \pm k$).
content_json.overview:
Fundamental Series Architectures:
- Arithmetic Progression (AP): $T_n = a + (n-1)d$
- Geometric Progression (GP): $T_n = a \cdot r^{n-1}$
- Two-Tier Differential Series: If first differences are not constant, computing second-order differences reveals a constant $d$ or AP
- Square and Cube Shift Series: $n^2 + 1, n^2 - 1, n^3 + 1, n^3 - 1, n^3 + n$
- Alternating / Dual Series: Two independent series interwoven at odd and even positions ($1, 4, 3, 9, 5, 16, 7 \dots$)
- Wrong Number Identification: Spotting the single outlier term violating the established recurrence relation

types.name: 1. Uniform & Variable Difference Series
types.desc: Sequences where consecutive terms increase or decrease by a constant or an AP of differences.
examples: 5, 9, 13, 17, 21 (+4 constant difference)
2, 5, 10, 17, 26 (Differences are +3, +5, +7, +9: consecutive odd numbers)

types.name: 2. Geometric & Ratio Multiplicative Series
types.desc: Terms formed by multiplying or dividing by a constant factor, or increasing multiplier sequence.
examples: 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 (*2 constant ratio)

types.name: 3. Two-Tier (Double Difference) Series
types.desc: Where first-level differences vary, but second-level differences reveal an arithmetic constancy.

types.name: 4. Power-Based (Square & Cube Shift) Series
types.desc: Terms directly related to squares or cubes of natural numbers with constant or variable additions.

types.name: 5. Alternating / Dual-Track Interleaved Series
types.desc: Two distinct series woven together at odd and even index positions.
examples: 2, 20, 4, 40, 6, 60, 8 (Odd positions: 2, 4, 6, 8; Even positions: 20, 40, 60)

rules.title: First-Tier vs Second-Tier Difference Method
rules.explanation: If a sequence grows moderately without sudden exponential jumps, write down the consecutive differences $\Delta_1 = T_{n+1} - T_n$. If $\Delta_1$ is not immediately obvious, calculate $\Delta_2 = \Delta_{1, n+1} - \Delta_{1, n}$. Over 70% of competitive series reduce to constant $\Delta_2$.
rules.correct: In 3, 8, 15, 24, 35: Diffs are 5, 7, 9, 11 (+2 constant). Next diff is 13 => 35 + 13 = 48.
rules.incorrect: Guessing multiplications when differences are simple AP.

rules.title: Exponential Jump Multiplicative Rule
rules.explanation: If consecutive terms jump rapidly (e.g. 5, 16, 51, 158), calculate the approximate ratio $T_{n+1} / T_n$. Look for patterns like $\times k \pm c$ (e.g. $\times 3 + 1$).
rules.incorrect: Attempting simple subtraction when terms triple at each step.

rules.title: Alternating Series Identification Rule
rules.explanation: If a sequence alternates between going up and going down (e.g. 10, 15, 12, 18, 14, 21), it is almost always TWO independent series interwoven. Separate odd-indexed and even-indexed elements.
rules.incorrect: Attempting a single unified difference (+5, -3, +6, -4, +7).

rules.title: Square & Cube Benchmark Recognition
rules.correct: Seeing 68, 130, 222 instantly triggers n^3 + n (4^3+4, 5^3+5, 6^3+6).
rules.incorrect: Calculating differences 62, 92 and wasting 2 minutes.

rules.title: Wrong Number in Series Detection Rule
rules.explanation: When identifying a wrong term in a series, remember that ONE incorrect number corrupts TWO consecutive difference values. The erroneous term is the one sandwiched between the two invalid differences.
rules.correct: Differences are 4, 6, 9, 11 (expecting 4, 6, 8, 10). The error is between 9 and 11.
rules.incorrect: Changing the first number when the error is in the middle.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying multiplication when terms only increase by single/double digits.
common_mistakes.correction: Always calculate differences first unless numbers jump by factors of 2x or 3x.
common_mistakes.rationale: Differences solve over 70% of standard series questions in SSC and Bank exams.

common_mistakes.mistake: Missing interleaved dual series when numbers fluctuate up and down.
common_mistakes.correction: Whenever a series rises then falls, immediately test splitting odd and even positions.
common_mistakes.rationale: Prevents complex oscillatory difference calculations.

common_mistakes.mistake: Failing to check $n^3 \pm n$ or $n^2 \pm n$ for numbers near cubes.
common_mistakes.correction: Check whether numbers like 30, 68, 130 match $n^3 + n$.
common_mistakes.rationale: Standard SSC CGL Tier 2 pattern.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the next term in a prime series is an odd composite number like 9, 15, or 21.
common_mistakes.correction: Remember that 2 is prime, and 9, 15, 21, 25, 27 are composite.
common_mistakes.rationale: Series 2, 3, 5, 7 is followed by 11, NOT 9.

quick_revision_points: Difference table is your #1 diagnostic tool for all non-exponential series
Rapid growth (2x, 3x, 4x) implies multiplication: test *k + c or *k - c
Fluctuating series (up, down, up, down) implies two interleaved independent series
In wrong number problems, the faulty number sits between the two faulty differences

lessons.title: Alphabet Series: Positional Ranks, Reverse Symmetry & Continuous Letter Patterns

content_json.definition: Alphabet Series problems evaluate patterns formed by English alphabet characters, tracking forward positions ($A=1 \dots Z=26$), reverse rankings ($Z=1 \dots A=26$), circular cyclical modulo shifts, opposite letter pairings (sum = 27), and continuous repeating letter sequences ($a\_b\_a\_$). Standard across SSC CGL, CHSL, RRB, and Banking exams, these tests assess quick conversion between letters and their positional integers.
content_json.overview:
Essential Alphabetical Frameworks:
- Forward Rank (A=1, B=2 ... Z=26) via EJOTY benchmarks (E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25) and CFILORUX (multiples of 3)
- Reverse Rank: $\text{Reverse Rank} = 27 - \text{Forward Rank}$
- Reverse Opposite Letter Pairs: AZ, BY, CX, DW, EV, FU, GT, HS, IR, JQ, KP, LO, MN
- Circular Wrap: Moving past Z wraps to A ($Z+1=A, Z+2=B$); moving before A wraps to Z ($A-1=Z$)
- Continuous Pattern Series: Dividing a sequence of length $N$ (e.g. 12, 15, 16, 20) into uniform blocks of 3, 4, or 5 characters to identify periodic cycles

types.name: 1. Uniform Single-Letter Step Series
types.desc: Individual letters increasing or decreasing by constant or AP step sizes.
examples: A, D, G, J, M (+3 steps: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13; next is P=16)

types.name: 2. Multi-Letter Cluster Series
types.desc: Groups of 2, 3, or 4 letters where each position follows an independent arithmetic progression.
examples: AB, CD, EF, GH (First letters +2, second letters +2)
ZAR, YBS, XCT (First letter -1, second letter +1, third letter +1)

types.name: 3. Opposite Letter Symmetry Series
types.desc: Series constructed using pairs whose ranks sum to 27.
examples: AZ, BY, CX, DW (A-Z, B-Y, C-X, D-W; next is EV)

types.name: 4. Continuous Repeating Pattern Series
types.desc: Sequences with blanks requiring block factorization (e.g., $16 = 4 \times 4$ or $15 = 5 \times 3$).
examples: ab_a_b_ab_a => factoring into blocks of 3 gives: aba, aba, aba, aba
_bc_ca_ab_ => factoring into abc, bca, cab (cyclic permutation)

types.name: 5. Alpha-Numeric Combination Series
types.desc: Letters combined with numbers representing their positions, squares, or differences.
examples: A2, C4, E8, G16 (Letters skip +2: A, C, E, G; Numbers double: 2, 4, 8, 16)

rules.title: EJOTY & CFILORUX Benchmark Rule
rules.explanation:
Never count letters on fingers from A. Use standard 5-step and 3-step anchors:
- EJOTY: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25
- CFILORUX: C=3, F=6, I=9, L=12, O=15, R=18, U=21, X=24.
rules.correct: To find rank of S: T is 20, so S = 20 - 1 = 19.
rules.incorrect: Counting A, B, C, D... on fingers taking 15 seconds.

rules.title: Reverse Opposite Sum 27 Rule
rules.explanation: The reverse counterpart of any letter with rank $R$ is $27 - R$. For example, the opposite of G (rank 7) is $27 - 7 = 20$ (T). Pairs are: AZ, BY, CX, DW, EV, FU, GT, HS, IR, JQ, KP, LO, MN.
rules.correct: Opposite of K (11) is 27 - 11 = 16 (P) => KP.
rules.incorrect: Subtracting from 26 giving 15 (O).

rules.title: Continuous Pattern Block Division Rule
rules.explanation: When solving repeating series like $a\_bc\_a\_$: (1) Count total characters including blanks ($N$). (2) Factorize $N$: if $N=12$, divide into $3 \times 4$ or $4 \times 3$; if $N=16$, divide into $4 \times 4$; if $N=15$, divide into $3 \times 5$ or $5 \times 3$. Check for identical or cyclical blocks.
rules.correct: Series of 16 characters: split into 4 blocks of 4 each to immediately see repeating pattern.
rules.incorrect: Trial and error by plugging in each of the 4 answer choices one by one.

rules.title: Independent Multi-Track Letter Position Rule
rules.explanation: In 3-letter cluster series (e.g. BDF, EGI, HJL), do NOT connect the letters within a cluster. Treat the 1st letters as Track 1 (B, E, H -> +3), 2nd letters as Track 2 (D, G, J -> +3), and 3rd letters as Track 3 (F, I, L -> +3).
rules.incorrect: Analyzing B to D (+2), D to F (+2), then trying to connect F to E (-1).

rules.title: Modular Alphabet Wrap-Around Rule
rules.explanation: Alphabet operations are modulo 26: $Z + 1 = A$ ($26 + 1 = 1$), $Z + 2 = B$, $A - 1 = Z$ ($1 - 1 = 26$). When an addition exceeds 26, subtract 26; when a subtraction goes below 1, add 26.
rules.incorrect: Stopping at Z and getting stuck.

common_mistakes.mistake: Counting letter positions from A on fingers during time-pressured exams.
common_mistakes.correction: Use EJOTY (5, 10, 15, 20, 25) to immediately determine any letter's position within 1 second.
common_mistakes.rationale: Saves 10-15 seconds per question and eliminates counting errors.

common_mistakes.mistake: Testing answer options blindly in continuous pattern series.
common_mistakes.correction: Count total length N and factorize into equal blocks (4x4, 3x5).
common_mistakes.rationale: Blind plugging takes 2 minutes; block division solves the pattern in 20 seconds.

common_mistakes.mistake: Subtracting from 26 instead of 27 to find reverse ranks.
common_mistakes.correction: Always subtract from 27 because the 1st letter (A=1) corresponds to the 26th letter (Z=26), giving 1 + 26 = 27.
common_mistakes.rationale: Mathematical principle of dual-ended index numbering.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing internal cluster relation with sequence-level progression.
common_mistakes.correction: Track first letters across all terms, then second letters across all terms.
common_mistakes.rationale: Inter-cluster tracking is the standard exam design pattern.

quick_revision_points: Opposite letter pairs sum to 27: AZ, BY, CX, DW, EV, FU, GT, HS, IR, JQ, KP, LO, MN
Reverse position of any letter = 27 - Forward position
Circular wrap: Z+1 = A, Z+2 = B; A-1 = Z, A-2 = Y
For continuous series: count total length, divide into blocks of 3, 4, or 5
Multi-letter clusters: solve position-by-position (all 1st letters, then all 2nd letters)
Vowel positions: A=1, E=5, I=9, O=15, U=21

lessons.title: Coding-Decoding: Letter Shifting, Substitution, Reverse Ranks & Matrix Rules

content_json.definition: Coding-Decoding evaluates cryptographic translation mechanisms where plain text words, numbers, or phrases are encrypted into cyphertext according to specific deterministic rules. Crucial in SSC CGL, IBPS/SBI PO, and Railways examinations, questions test forward/reverse rank shifting ($+k, -k$), opposite letter substitution (sum = 27), cross-positional rearrangement, direct symbol substitution, Chinese sentence elimination, and conditional matrix coding.
content_json.overview:
Fundamental Cryptographic Patterns:
- Direct Letter Shifting: Constant shift (e.g. $+2$ to every letter), alternating shifts ($+1, -1, +1, -1$), or progressive shifts ($+1, +2, +3, +4$)
- Reverse Opposite Pairing: Replacing each letter with its opposite (A with Z, B with Y, C with X)
- Cross-Positional Scrambling: Swapping adjacent pairs (e.g., positions $1 \leftrightarrow 2, 3 \leftrightarrow 4$) or reversing the entire word
- Number / Sum of Ranks Coding: Coding words by total sum of letter ranks (CAT = $3+1+20=24$) or sum of opposite ranks
- Substitution / Chinese Coding: Comparing multiple phrases ('she is good', 'good and sweet') to isolate individual word meanings via intersection

types.name: 1. Positional Shift & Progressive Coding
types.desc: Letters shifted by fixed constants or linearly increasing step increments.
examples: If TEACHER is coded as VGCEJGT (+2 shift to every letter)
If DELHI is coded as EFMIJ (+1 shift to every letter)

types.name: 2. Reverse Alphabetical & Opposite Letter Coding
types.desc: Encoding characters into their mirror counterparts where $R_1 + R_2 = 27$.
examples: If KING is coded as PRMT (K-P, I-R, N-M, G-T are opposite pairs)
If HAND is coded as SZMW (H-S, A-Z, N-M, D-W)

types.name: 3. Letter-to-Number / Value Aggregation Coding
types.desc: Converting words into numeric quantities via rank summation, multiplication, or vowel/consonant weighting.
examples: If CAT = 24 (3+1+20) and DOG = 26 (4+15+7), find PET
If GO = 32 (Opposites of G=20, O=12; 20+12 = 32)

types.name: 4. Fictitious Language / Chinese Coding
types.desc: Finding code-word correspondence by eliminating shared tokens across multiple sentences.
examples: 'pic vic nic' = 'winter is cold'; 'ri nic to' = 'summer is hot' => common word 'is' = 'nic'
Isolating unique terms by set difference

types.name: 5. Conditional Matrix & Rule-Based Coding
types.desc: Applying conditional rules (e.g., if first letter is vowel and last is consonant, swap codes).
examples: Conditional digit coding in Bank PO examinations

rules.title: Check Shift Homogeneity Rule
rules.explanation: Before assuming a constant shift (like $+2$), calculate the shift for the first 3 letters. If shifts are $+1, +2, +3$, it is a progressive series; if $+2, -2, +2, -2$, it is alternating.
rules.correct: In LIGHT -> MJJIW: L(+1)->M, I(+1)->J, G(+3)->J? Verify exact differences for all letters.
rules.incorrect: Checking only the first letter and assuming the entire word follows the same shift.

rules.title: Opposite Sum 27 Value Check
rules.explanation: When numeric codes seem unusually high for small words (e.g., GO = 32, when standard ranks are G=7, O=15 giving 22), check the sum of the OPPOSITE ranks: Opposite of G is T(20), opposite of O is L(12). $20 + 12 = 32$.
rules.incorrect: Assuming arbitrary addition of +10 without checking opposite letter ranks.

rules.title: Chinese Coding Sentence Intersection Rule
rules.explanation: To decode fictitious language words: (1) Find a pair of sentences that share exactly ONE English word. (2) Find the single code token common to both code sentences. (3) That common token is the definitive translation.
rules.correct: Sentence 1: 'sky is blue' = 'ti ka pa'; Sentence 2: 'blue sea' = 'pa lo'. Common word 'blue' = common code 'pa'.
rules.incorrect: Assuming words and codes appear in the identical left-to-right order.

rules.title: Cross-Positional Inversion Pattern Rule
rules.explanation: If the letters in the cyphertext are an exact anagram of the original word, the encryption is purely positional transposition (not rank shifting). Number positions 1 to $N$ and map the permutation.
rules.correct: MOTHER -> REHTOM (Word is simply reversed from end to start).
rules.incorrect: Calculating shifts between M and R.

rules.title: Direct Symbol / Alphabet Mapping Rule
rules.explanation: If two example words share common letters that map to the identical symbols/letters (e.g. in FIRE = #$%* and RAIN = *&!^, 'R' is '*' in both), the code is direct 1-to-1 letter mapping without arithmetic operations.
rules.correct: Identifying that each letter in the target word already appears in the given examples and directly copying codes.
rules.incorrect: Searching for complex mathematical rules when it is a direct lookup table.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming word order matches code order in Chinese/Fictitious coding.
common_mistakes.correction: Words are intentionally scrambled. You must use intersection across sentences.
common_mistakes.rationale: 'sky is blue' does not mean 'sky' is the first code word.

common_mistakes.mistake: Testing only the first letter's shift and selecting an answer option too quickly.
common_mistakes.correction: Always verify at least the first two and the last letter of the word.
common_mistakes.rationale: Examiners intentionally design options where the first letter matches multiple distractors.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting opposite letter ranks when numeric sum doesn't match standard forward ranks.
common_mistakes.correction: If forward ranks sum to 22 but code is 32, immediately test reverse ranks (27 - R).
common_mistakes.rationale: Standard high-yield banking examination trick.

common_mistakes.mistake: Trying letter shift formulas on transposition/anagram codes.
common_mistakes.correction: If the cyphertext uses the exact same letters as the plaintext, map position indices.
common_mistakes.rationale: Saves up to 1 minute per question.

quick_revision_points: Always check first: Are the cypher letters identical to original letters? If yes => Transposition
Are two examples given with identical letter-to-code mapping? If yes => Direct substitution
Is the code a number? Check: (1) Sum of forward ranks (2) Sum of opposite ranks (3) Number of letters
Opposite letter pairs sum to 27: AZ, BY, CX, DW, EV, FU, GT, HS, IR, JQ, KP, LO, MN
Chinese coding: Compare two sentences at a time to eliminate common terms
EJOTY benchmarks: E=5, J=10, O=15, T=20, Y=25
Progressive shifts (+1, +2, +3...) are common in SSC CGL Tier 1

lessons.title: Blood Relations: Family Tree Diagrams, Coded Genealogies & Conversational Puzzles

content_json.definition: Blood Relations in competitive examinations evaluate the capacity to trace and decode multi-generational biological and matrimonial lineages through symbolic representations or conversational references. Evaluated across SSC CGL, IBPS/SBI PO, RRB, and State PSCs, problems encompass generation-level hierarchies, gender determination rules, coded algebraic relationships ($P \times Q \implies P \text{ is mother of } Q$), and direct pointing/portrait conversational deductions.
content_json.overview:
Essential Lineage Rules & Standard Notation:
- Gender Notation: Square / Plus sign $[+]$ for Male; Circle / Minus sign $[-]$ for Female
- Matrimonial Link: Double horizontal line $(=)$ between husband and wife
- Sibling Link: Single horizontal line $(-)$ with bracket
- Generational Step: Vertical line $(\mid)$ descending from parent to child
- Generation Levels:
  - Level +2: Grandparents (Paternal / Maternal grandfather & grandmother)
  - Level +1: Parents, Uncles, Aunts (Paternal: Chacha, Tau, Bua; Maternal: Mama, Mami, Mausi)
  - Level 0: Self, Spouse, Siblings, Cousins, Brother-in-law, Sister-in-law
  - Level -1: Children, Nephews, Nieces
  - Level -2: Grandchildren (Grandson, Granddaughter)

types.name: 1. Pointing / Portrait Conversational Questions
types.desc: Deducing relationships when a speaker points to a photograph or person ('He is the only son of my father's father').
examples: 'The only son of my grandfather' = Speaker's Father
'Daughter of the only son of my grandfather' = Speaker's Sister (or Self if female)

types.name: 2. Coded Blood Relations
types.desc: Lineage chains described using mathematical or punctuation operators (e.g. $A + B$ means $A$ is sister of $B$).
examples: Evaluate $P \div Q - R + S$ by decoding step-by-step from left to right
Determine which expression proves $M$ is the maternal uncle of $N$

types.name: 3. Multi-Member Family Tree Puzzles
types.desc: Complex family structures involving 6-8 members across 3 generations with married couples and professions.
examples: 3 married couples in a 7-member family: building the complete generational tree
Identifying the number of male and female members in the household

types.name: 4. Maternal vs Paternal Relationship Distinctions
types.desc: Distinguishing relations on the father's side (Paternal) versus the mother's side (Maternal).
examples: Father's brother = Paternal Uncle; Mother's brother = Maternal Uncle
Father's sister's son = Paternal Cousin; Mother's sister = Maternal Aunt

types.name: 5. In-Law Matrimonial Relationships
types.desc: Relations formed through marriage (Spouse's siblings, Sibling's spouses, Children's spouses).
examples: Sister-in-law: Husband's sister, Wife's sister, Brother's wife
Brother-in-law: Husband's brother, Wife's brother, Sister's husband

rules.title: Never Assume Gender from a Name Rule
rules.explanation: In competitive exams, gender CANNOT be inferred from traditional human names (e.g., 'Kiran', 'Suman', 'Bobby', 'Raman'). Gender MUST be explicitly stated through pronouns (he/she), titles (father, sister), or matrimonial pairing (husband implies the other spouse is female).
rules.correct: 'A is the child of B' leaves A's gender undetermined unless 'A is the son' or 'A is brother' is stated.
rules.incorrect: Assuming 'Pooja' is female without explicit textual proof.

rules.title: 'Only Son / Daughter' Deductive Rule
rules.explanation:
- 'Only son of my father' = The speaker himself (if speaker is male) or the speaker's brother (if speaker is female).
- 'Only child of my father' = The speaker himself/herself (strictly unique offspring).
- 'My father's only son's wife' = Speaker's wife (if male) or Sister-in-law (if female).
rules.correct: Male speaker says: 'His mother is the only daughter of my mother.' My mother's only daughter = My sister. Thus, his mother is my sister => I am his Maternal Uncle.
rules.incorrect: Equating 'only son' with 'only child' (ignoring potential sisters).

rules.title: Coded Relations Gender and Generation Gap Elimination
rules.explanation:
When asked 'Which option proves $M$ is female?':
1. Eliminate options where $M$ is at the very end of an expression without a following operator (gender usually unknown).
2. Eliminate options where $M$'s operator assigns a male gender ($M$ is father/brother).
3. Check generation gap: $Father (+1), Son (-1), Sister (0)$. Total sum must match the target gap.
rules.correct: If $M$ must be female, eliminate option $M \times K$ where '$\times$' means 'is brother of'.
rules.incorrect: Drawing complete family trees for all 4 options, wasting 3 minutes.

rules.title: Backward Parsing in Pointing Problems
rules.explanation:
In statements like 'He is the son of the daughter of the father of my wife': Start parsing from the end ('my wife') backwards step-by-step:
1. 'My wife'
2. 'Father of my wife' = Father-in-law
3. 'Daughter of my father-in-law' = Wife (or Sister-in-law)
4. 'Son of my wife' = Son.
rules.correct: Parsing backwards from 'my' breaks the sentence into 4 instant simplifications.
rules.incorrect: Trying to translate the sentence from the first word forward.

rules.title: Matrimonial Implied Gender Complementarity
rules.explanation: In standard biological family reasoning problems, marriage is heterosexual. If member $A$ is the husband, spouse $B$ is definitively female (wife). Conversely, if $B$ is the wife, $A$ is definitively male (husband).
rules.correct: If A is married to B and A is the father of C, then B is definitively the mother of C (Female).
rules.incorrect: Leaving B's gender as unknown.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the speaker is male when not specified.
common_mistakes.correction: Always check both possibilities (speaker is male or female) if gender is not fixed.
common_mistakes.rationale: 'The only daughter of my mother' is the speaker herself if female, but the speaker's sister if male.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing Paternal and Maternal relatives.
common_mistakes.correction: Paternal relates to Father (Chacha/Bua); Maternal relates to Mother (Mama/Mausi).
common_mistakes.rationale: High-frequency trap in bilingual SSC and State exams.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating 'Cousin' as having a gender.
common_mistakes.correction: Cousin is a gender-neutral term covering both male and female relatives.
common_mistakes.rationale: Never say 'Cousin brother' or 'Cousin sister' in formal reasoning.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing whole trees instead of using gender elimination in coded relations.
common_mistakes.correction: Check the candidate's immediate gender operator first to eliminate 2-3 options in 10 seconds.
common_mistakes.rationale: Saves 80% of test time in Bank PO / SSC Tier 2.

quick_revision_points: Use standard tree symbols: Square = Male, Circle = Female, '=' = Married, '|' = Generation shift
Never assume gender from a proper name without an explicit relationship tag
'Only child' means zero brothers and zero sisters; 'Only son' allows multiple sisters
Backward parsing: start from 'my' and simplify right-to-left
Generation Gaps: Grandparents (+2), Parents (+1), Siblings/Spouse/Cousins (0), Children (-1)
Nephew = Brother's or Sister's Son; Niece = Brother's or Sister's Daughter
Uncle's or Aunt's child is always a COUSIN

lessons.title: Direction Sense: Compass Navigation, Pythagoras Displacement & Shadow Logic

content_json.definition: Direction Sense tests spatial orientation, path tracing across an 8-point Cartesian compass, net displacement calculation via the Pythagorean Theorem, and solar shadow position deductions. Prominent in SSC CGL Tier 1/2, IBPS/SBI PO, and Railways examinations, questions examine sequential right/left turns, clockwise/counter-clockwise angular rotations ($45^\circ, 90^\circ, 135^\circ, 180^\circ$), and sunrise/sunset shadow angles.
content_json.overview:
Essential Compass System & Rules:
- 4 Main Cardinal Directions: North (Up / $0^\circ$), East (Right / $90^\circ$), South (Down / $180^\circ$), West (Left / $270^\circ$)
- 4 Intercardinal Directions: North-East (NE / $45^\circ$), South-East (SE / $135^\circ$), South-West (SW / $225^\circ$), North-West (NW / $315^\circ$)
- Turn Conventions:
  - Right Turn = $90^\circ$ Clockwise (CW)
  - Left Turn = $90^\circ$ Anti-Clockwise (ACW)
- Pythagorean Shortest Distance: $\text{Displacement } D = \sqrt{(\Sigma X)^2 + (\Sigma Y)^2}$
- Shadow Rules:
  - At Sunrise (Sun in East): Shadows fall strictly to the WEST
  - At Sunset (Sun in West): Shadows fall strictly to the EAST
  - At 12:00 Noon: The sun is directly overhead; NO horizontal shadow is cast

types.name: 1. Multi-Step Distance & Path Trajectory
types.desc: Walking successive distances in cardinal directions to determine final position relative to start point.
examples: Walks 10m North, turns right walks 5m, turns right walks 10m => 5m East of start point
Net coordinate cancellation: +10 North and -10 South cancel out

types.name: 2. Shortest Distance (Pythagoras Theorem)
types.desc: Calculating straight-line Euclidean displacement between starting point and endpoint.
examples: Walks 3 km East, then 4 km North: D = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(25) = 5 km North-East
Walks 6 km West, then 8 km South: D = sqrt(6^2 + 8^2) = 10 km South-West

types.name: 3. Angular Rotation & Headings
types.desc: Person turns through specific angles clockwise or counter-clockwise from an initial heading.
examples: Facing North, turns 90 deg CW (East), then 135 deg ACW (North-West)
Net rotation = Sum of CW - Sum of ACW

types.name: 4. Sunrise and Sunset Shadow Problems
types.desc: Deducing facing direction from the orientation of a shadow (to one's left, right, front, or back).
examples: At sunrise, if shadow is to your right => You are facing South
At sunrise, if shadow is to your left => You are facing North

types.name: 5. Coded Direction & Distance Puzzles
types.desc: Direction relationships encoded using symbols (e.g. $P @ Q$ means $P$ is 6m North of $Q$).
examples: High-level Bank PO puzzles mapping multiple points in a coordinate grid

rules.title: Turn Relativity Depends on Current Facing Heading
rules.explanation:
- Facing North: Right = East, Left = West
- Facing South: Right = West, Left = East (Reversed!)
- Facing East: Right = South, Left = North
- Facing West: Right = North, Left = South.
rules.correct: When facing South, taking a Right turn points you WEST.
rules.incorrect: Assuming Right turn is always East regardless of facing direction.

rules.title: Pythagoras Displacement Formula
rules.explanation: The straight-line shortest distance $D$ between origin $(0,0)$ and final coordinates $(x, y)$ is given by $D = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$. Memorize common Pythagorean triplets: $(3, 4, 5)$, $(5, 12, 13)$, $(6, 8, 10)$, $(8, 15, 17)$, $(7, 24, 25)$.
rules.correct: Net displacement 5m East and 12m North => D = sqrt(25 + 144) = 13m.
rules.incorrect: Adding distances arithmetically (5 + 12 = 17m).

rules.title: Sunrise & Sunset Shadow Matrix Rule
rules.explanation:
- **At Sunrise (Sun in East => Shadow falls West)**:
  - Facing North $\implies$ Shadow to Left
  - Facing South $\implies$ Shadow to Right
  - Facing East $\implies$ Shadow Behind
  - Facing West $\implies$ Shadow in Front
- **At Sunset (Sun in West => Shadow falls East)**:
  - Facing North $\implies$ Shadow to Right
  - Facing South $\implies$ Shadow to Left.
rules.correct: One morning, Amit's shadow was exactly to his left. Thus, Amit was facing North.
rules.incorrect: Saying Amit was facing East.

rules.title: Net Angular Rotation Shortcut
rules.explanation:
When multiple turns are made:
$\text{Net Rotation} = \sum (\text{Clockwise Angles}) - \sum (\text{Anti-Clockwise Angles})$.
If the result is positive, turn that angle Clockwise from the starting heading. If negative, turn Anti-Clockwise.
rules.correct: Facing East. Turns 45 CW, then 90 CW, then 180 ACW: Net = (45 + 90) - 180 = 135 - 180 = -45 (45 ACW). East rotated 45 ACW = North-East.
rules.incorrect: Redrawing the entire figure 3 times.

rules.title: Origin vs Current Heading Distinction
rules.explanation:
Exams ask two distinct questions:
(1) 'In which direction is he from the STARTING point?' (Requires vector from origin $(0,0)$ to final $(x,y)$).
(2) 'In which direction is he now FACING?' (Requires only the last heading after the final turn).
rules.correct: Final position is (5m East, 0m North), but person turned South at the end: From start point = East; Facing = South.
rules.incorrect: Confusing the direction from start point with the facing direction.

common_mistakes.mistake: Adding path distances linearly when asked for 'shortest distance'.
common_mistakes.correction: Shortest distance is the hypotenuse $D = \sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2}$, not total path traveled.
common_mistakes.rationale: Exam questions deliberately offer total path distance as Option A.

common_mistakes.mistake: Turning Right towards East when facing South.
common_mistakes.correction: When facing South, turning Right moves you WEST.
common_mistakes.rationale: Turning Right is clockwise. From South ($180^\circ$), CW brings you to West ($270^\circ$).

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming shadows fall in the direction of the sun.
common_mistakes.correction: Shadows fall strictly in the direction OPPOSITE to the sun (Sun in East => Shadow in West).
common_mistakes.rationale: Light travel physics rule.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing 'Facing direction' with 'Direction from starting point'.
common_mistakes.correction: Check the exact question prompt: 'facing' vs 'with respect to starting position'.
common_mistakes.rationale: High-frequency trap in competitive reasoning tests.

quick_revision_points: Cardinal: North (Up), South (Down), East (Right), West (Left)
Intercardinal: NE, SE, SW, NW (each at 45 degrees)
Right turn = 90 deg Clockwise; Left turn = 90 deg Anti-Clockwise
Sunrise: Sun = East, Shadow = West. Facing North => Shadow to Left; Facing South => Shadow to Right
Sunset: Sun = West, Shadow = East. Facing North => Shadow to Right; Facing South => Shadow to Left
Net angle = Total CW - Total ACW

lessons.title: Ranking & Order: Linear Queues, Position Interchanging & Overlapping Logic

content_json.definition: Ranking and Order evaluates positional logic within finite ordered sequences (queues, classroom merit lists, seating rows). Tested rigorously in SSC CGL, IBPS/SBI Clerk, RRB, and State PSCs, problems require calculating total strength $T = (L + R) - 1$, finding rank from opposite ends, determining person counts between two ranked individuals, solving position interchanging dilemmas, and analyzing overlapping vs non-overlapping queue configurations.
content_json.overview:
Fundamental Ranking Formulas:
- Total Number in a Single Row: $T = \text{Rank from Left } (L) + \text{Rank from Right } (R) - 1$
- Rank from Opposite End:
  - $L = (T - R) + 1$
  - $R = (T - L) + 1$
- Persons Between Two Individuals (Non-Overlapping): $\text{Middle} = T - (L_A + R_B)$ (Valid when $T > L_A + R_B$)
- Persons Between Two Individuals (Overlapping Case): $\text{Middle} = (L_A + R_B) - T - 2$ (Valid when $L_A + R_B > T$)
- Minimum Number of Persons in Row: $T_{\text{min}} = (L_A + R_B) - \text{Middle} - 2$

types.name: 1. Single Person Bidirectional Ranking
types.desc: Calculating total persons or rank from one end when a single person's rank from both ends is known.
examples: Ravi is 10th from left and 15th from right: Total = 10 + 15 - 1 = 24
Total 50 students, Priya is 18th from top: Rank from bottom = (50 - 18) + 1 = 33

types.name: 2. Position Interchanging Dilemmas
types.desc: Two individuals swap positions, revealing a new rank that allows determining total strength.
examples: A (10th from left) swaps with B (9th from right). A is now 15th from left => Total = 15 + 9 - 1 = 23

types.name: 3. Between / Middle Count (Non-Overlapping vs Overlapping)
types.desc: Finding the number of individuals seated between two distinct people.
examples: Total 40. A is 10th from left, B is 12th from right. Between = 40 - (10 + 12) = 18
Total 20. A is 14th from left, B is 12th from right. Overlapping between = (14 + 12) - 20 - 2 = 4

types.name: 4. Comparative Vertical Order Ranking
types.desc: Ordering individuals by height, weight, marks, or age using inequality chains ($A > B \ge C$).
examples: A is taller than B but shorter than C. D is shorter than B. Tallest is C

types.name: 5. Maximum and Minimum Row Strength
types.desc: Calculating theoretical extreme queue capacities given two ranks and intermediate people.
examples: Max capacity = L + R + Middle
Min capacity = (L + R) - Middle - 2

rules.title: Minus One Double-Counting Rule
rules.explanation: When summing a person's rank from the left and right ($L + R$), that specific person is counted TWICE (once in the left group and once in the right group). Therefore, 1 must ALWAYS be subtracted: $T = L + R - 1$.
rules.correct: Rank 7th from left and 12th from right: Total = 7 + 12 - 1 = 18.
rules.incorrect: Adding 7 + 12 = 19 (counting the student twice).

rules.title: Plus One Opposite Rank Conversion Rule
rules.explanation: To find rank from the opposite end given total $T$ and rank $R$: $\text{Opposite Rank} = (T - R) + 1$. You must add 1 back because subtracting $R$ removes the person themselves from the remaining count.
rules.correct: In a row of 30, rank from left is 8: Rank from right = (30 - 8) + 1 = 23.
rules.incorrect: Calculating 30 - 8 = 22.

rules.title: Position Interchanging Master Rule
rules.explanation: When person $A$ and person $B$ interchange seats, the NEW position of $A$ coincides with the ORIGINAL position of $B$. Therefore: $\text{Total} = \text{New Rank of } A + \text{Old Rank of } B - 1$.
rules.correct: A is 12th left, B is 18th right. They swap. A is now 20th left: Total = 20 + 18 - 1 = 37.
rules.incorrect: Adding old A and old B.

rules.title: Overlapping Condition Test $(L + R > T)$
rules.explanation:
Check if $(L_A + R_B) > T$:
- If $L_A + R_B < T \implies$ Simple non-overlapping queue: $\text{Between} = T - (L_A + R_B)$.
- If $L_A + R_B > T \implies$ Overlapping queue where $A$ and $B$ cross each other: $\text{Between} = (L_A + R_B) - T - 2$. (The 2 accounts for $A$ and $B$ being recounted).
rules.correct: Total 25. A is 16th left, B is 14th right. 16+14=30 > 25 (Overlapping!). Between = 30 - 25 - 2 = 3.
rules.incorrect: Calculating 30 - 25 = 5 (forgetting to subtract 2 for the cross-count of A and B).

rules.title: Shift / Insertion Shift Rule
rules.explanation: If a person is shifted by $k$ places towards the left, their rank from the left DECREASES by $k$, and their rank from the right INCREASES by $k$. Total number in row remains unchanged.
rules.correct: P is 14th from left. Shifted 3 places left => New left rank = 14 - 3 = 11.
rules.incorrect: Adding 3 when shifting left.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the '- 1' in Total = Left + Right.
common_mistakes.correction: Always apply T = L + R - 1 because the anchor person is counted in both directions.
common_mistakes.rationale: Most common source of +1 mark deductions in competitive ranking tests.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the '- 2' in overlapping between-count formula.
common_mistakes.correction: Between = (L + R) - T - 2. You must subtract 2 because both individuals are counted in both spans.
common_mistakes.rationale: Crucial distinction between standard and overlapping queues.

common_mistakes.mistake: Calculating rank from right as simply Total - Left.
common_mistakes.correction: Right rank = (Total - Left) + 1.
common_mistakes.rationale: Subtracting Left eliminates the person, so you must add 1 to place them in the queue.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming non-overlapping without checking L + R against Total.
common_mistakes.correction: Always compare (L + R) with Total first before choosing the formula.
common_mistakes.rationale: Prevents negative values or incorrect between counts.

quick_revision_points: Total T = Left + Right - 1
Left = (Total - Right) + 1; Right = (Total - Left) + 1
Non-overlapping (T > L + R): Between = T - (L + R)
Overlapping (L + R > T): Between = (L + R) - T - 2
Minimum strength: T_min = (L + R) - Between - 2
Maximum strength: T_max = L + R + Between
Position Swap: Total = New Rank of A + Old Rank of B - 1

lessons.title: Syllogism: Aristotelian Deductions, 'Only a Few', Possibility Cases & Complementary Pairs

content_json.definition: Syllogism evaluates deductive logical consequence where definite or probabilistic conclusions are evaluated strictly against given premises, irrespective of empirical real-world facts. Extensively tested across IBPS/SBI PO, SSC CGL Tier 1/2, CAT, and State Exams, modern syllogism incorporates traditional quantifiers (All, Some, No, Some Not), contemporary banking quantifiers ('Only a few', 'Only', 'At least'), possibility scenarios, and Either-Or complementary pairs.
content_json.overview:
Core Propositions & Distribution Logic:
- A-Type (Universal Affirmative): 'All $S$ are $P$' (Subject distributed, Predicate undistributed)
- E-Type (Universal Negative): 'No $S$ is $P$' (Both distributed)
- I-Type (Particular Affirmative): 'Some $S$ are $P$' (Neither distributed)
- O-Type (Particular Negative): 'Some $S$ are not $P$' (Predicate distributed)
- Modern Quantifier Translations:
  - 'Only a few A are B' $\equiv$ 'Some A are B' AND 'Some A are NOT B' (Dual statement!)
  - 'Only A are B' $\equiv$ 'All B are A' (Reversed universal affirmative)
  - 'At least some A are B' $\equiv$ 'Some A are B'
- Either-Or Complementary Pairs:
  - Pair 1: I + E ('Some A are B' + 'No A is B')
  - Pair 2: A + O ('All A are B' + 'Some A are not B')

types.name: 1. Standard Universal & Particular Categorical Syllogisms
types.desc: Traditional two-premise syllogisms with 'All', 'Some', and 'No'.
examples: Statements: All apples are fruits. All fruits are sweet. Conclusion: All apples are sweet (Definite True)
Statements: Some pens are books. Some books are pencils. Conclusion: Some pens are pencils (False/Doubtful)

types.name: 2. Modern Banking 'Only a Few' & 'Only' Syllogisms
types.desc: Propositions incorporating negative restriction alongside affirmative overlap.
examples: 'Only a few roses are red' implies (1) Some roses are red, AND (2) Some roses are definitely NOT red
'Only kings are brave' translates strictly to 'All brave are kings'

types.name: 3. Possibility & Can-Be Scenarios
types.desc: Evaluating whether a conclusion is feasible in at least one valid Venn diagram without violating premises.
examples: If 'Some A are B', then 'All A being B is a possibility' is TRUE
If 'No A is B', then 'Some A being B is a possibility' is FALSE

types.name: 4. Either-Or Complementary Pairs
types.desc: Two conclusions where both cannot be true together and both cannot be false together.
examples: 1. Some cats are dogs. 2. No cat is a dog. (Subject & Predicate same, one +ve one -ve, both doubtful => Either 1 or 2 follows)

types.name: 5. Negative / Does Not Follow Syllogisms
types.desc: Identifying which conclusion definitively FAILS or cannot hold under any interpretation.
examples: Testing which statement violates the minimum overlapping Venn boundary

rules.title: 'Only a Few' Dual-Statement Rule
rules.explanation:
The quantifier 'Only a few $A$ are $B$' contains TWO simultaneous premises:
(1) **Some $A$ are $B$** (Positive overlap)
(2) **Some $A$ are NOT $B$** (Definite negative exclusion).
Therefore: The conclusion 'All $A$ can be $B$' is ALWAYS FALSE, while 'All $B$ can be $A$' is a valid possibility.
words: Only a Few = Some + Some Not
All A can be B is FALSE
rules.correct: Given 'Only a few cats are dogs': 'All dogs being cats is a possibility' is TRUE; 'All cats being dogs is a possibility' is FALSE.
rules.incorrect: Treating 'Only a few' as identical to regular 'Some'.

rules.title: Either-Or Three Golden Conditions
rules.explanation:
Either-Or applies between Conclusion 1 and Conclusion 2 if and only if:
1. Both individual conclusions are **Indeterminate / Doubtful** (cannot be definitely proved from premises).
2. They share the **identical Subject and Predicate**.
3. They form a valid **Complementary Pair**: (Some + No) or (All + Some Not).
*(Note: All + No is NOT an either-or pair!)*
rules.correct: 1. Some P are Q (Doubtful). 2. No P is Q (Doubtful). Result: Either 1 or 2 follows.
rules.incorrect: Applying Either-Or to 'All P are Q' and 'No P is Q' (both can be false simultaneously).

rules.title: Possibility Validity Rule
rules.explanation:
A conclusion stating '$X$ being $Y$ is a possibility' is **TRUE** if there is no direct contradiction in the premises. However:
- If a statement is ALREADY definitely true, its possibility is technically redundant/false in modern banking logic.
- If a statement is definitely impossible (violates a 'No' rule), its possibility is FALSE.
rules.correct: If Some A are B: 'All A being B is a possibility' is TRUE.
rules.incorrect: If No A is B: Claiming 'Some A being B is a possibility'.

rules.title: Universal Negative Definitive Boundary Rule
rules.explanation: If 'No $A$ is $B$', then no part of circle $A$ can ever intersect with circle $B$. Furthermore, if 'All $C$ are $A$', then automatically 'No $C$ is $B$'.
rules.correct: Statements: All cars are vehicles. No vehicle is a boat. Conclusion: No car is a boat (Definitively True).
rules.incorrect: Assuming cars could possibly intersect with boats.

rules.title: Disregard Real-World Empirical Truth Rule
rules.explanation: You must accept the premises as 100% indisputable facts, even if they contradict known physical reality (e.g., 'All dogs are trees'). Never reject a conclusion because it sounds absurd in real life.
rules.correct: All cats are chairs. All chairs are tables => All cats are tables (Valid logical conclusion).
rules.incorrect: Rejecting the conclusion because cats cannot be tables in real life.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating 'Only a few A are B' as simple 'Some A are B'.
common_mistakes.correction: Remember that 'Only a few' mandates that some A are strictly excluded from B.
common_mistakes.rationale: 'All A being B' is completely impossible under 'Only a few'.

common_mistakes.mistake: Selecting Either-Or for 'All A are B' and 'No A is B'.
common_mistakes.correction: All + No is contrary, not contradictory (both can be false). Valid pairs are (Some + No) and (All + Some Not).
common_mistakes.rationale: Classical formal logic rule.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming two 'Some' premises yield a definite conclusion.
common_mistakes.correction: Some + Some = No Definite Conclusion (only possibility conclusions can hold).
common_mistakes.rationale: Venn circles may or may not overlap.

common_mistakes.mistake: Allowing common sense or scientific facts to overrule stated premises.
common_mistakes.correction: Only evaluate formal deductive truth strictly based on the stated statements.
common_mistakes.rationale: Syllogism tests formal deductive validity, not factual accuracy.

quick_revision_points: 'Only a few A are B' = Some A are B + Some A are NOT B
'Only A are B' = All B are A
Either-Or pairs: (Some + No) or (All + Some Not)
All + No is NEVER an Either-Or pair
Some + Some gives NO definite conclusion
No + No gives NO definite conclusion
If a conclusion is already definitely true, it is not just a possibility

lessons.title: Venn Diagrams: Three-Entity Sets, Geometrical Regions & Set-Theoretic Deductions

content_json.definition: Venn Diagrams represent logical and set-theoretic relationships among classes or finite groups using enclosed plane figures (circles, squares, triangles, rectangles). Prominent across SSC CGL, RRB NTPC, State PSCs, and Defence exams, questions require mapping conceptual entity hierarchies (e.g. Earth, Asia, India) into representative topological figures, as well as reading multi-figure intersections to compute exact numerical populations ($n(A \cup B \cup C)$).
content_json.overview:
Essential Venn Archetypes & Set Formulas:
- Inclusive Subsets (Nested Circles): $A \subset B \subset C$ (e.g., Seconds $\subset$ Minutes $\subset$ Hours)
- Mutually Exclusive / Disjoint Sets: Completely separated circles (e.g., Cat, Dog, Bird)
- Partial Overlap (Intersection): Some elements shared (e.g., Doctors, Musicians, Teachers)
- Two-Group Set Formula: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$
- Three-Group Set Formula:
  $n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - [n(A \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(C \cap A)] + n(A \cap B \cap C)$
- Geometrical Diagram Analysis: Identifying numbers situated inside a triangle (e.g. Doctors) and square (e.g. Hardworking), but outside circle (e.g. Rural)

types.name: 1. Categorical / Taxonomic Class Representation
types.desc: Selecting the correct diagram illustrating relationships among three real-world entities.
examples: Mammals, Cow, Crow (Cow is inside Mammals; Crow is a disjoint bird circle)
State, Country, Continent (Three concentric nested circles)

types.name: 2. Intersecting Multi-Professional Sets
types.desc: Three partially overlapping circles depicting overlapping skills or professions.
examples: Authors, Teachers, Women (All three can partially intersect: a woman can be both an author and a teacher)

types.name: 3. Geometrical Figure Region Identification
types.desc: Reading labels from intersecting geometric shapes (Triangle = Teachers, Circle = Doctors, Rectangle = Rural).
examples: Find the number representing 'Doctors who are neither teachers nor rural'
Find the number representing 'Rural teachers who are also doctors'

types.name: 4. Set-Theoretic Arithmetic Equations
types.desc: Calculating 'Only A', 'Only B', or 'All three' given total demographic survey figures.
examples: In a class of 100: 60 play Cricket, 50 play Football, 20 play both. How many play neither?

types.name: 5. Two Enclosed and One Separated Group
types.desc: Two categories possessing an overlap while both being completely disjoint from a third.
examples: Dogs, Pets, Tables (Dogs and Pets overlap; Tables is completely separate)

rules.title: Universal Concentric Containment Rule
rules.explanation: If entity $A$ is a strict subset of $B$ and $B$ is a strict subset of $C$ ($A \subset B \subset C$), the diagram MUST be three concentric nested circles.
rules.correct: Seconds, Minutes, Hours: Seconds are inside Minutes, which are inside Hours.
rules.incorrect: Drawing three partially overlapping circles.

rules.title: Universal Disjoint Separation Rule
rules.explanation: If no member of entity $A$ can ever be a member of $B$ or $C$, and no members are shared among any pairs, the diagram MUST consist of three mutually separated, non-touching circles.
rules.correct: Chair, Table, Bed (All three are distinct pieces of furniture with zero common elements).
rules.incorrect: Intersecting chair and table.

rules.title: 'Only' Region Isolation Rule in Geometric Venn
rules.explanation: When asked for 'Only category $A$', look exclusively inside the region bounded by shape $A$ that does NOT intersect with ANY other geometric boundary.
rules.correct: In Circle (Athletes) and Triangle (Scholars): 'Only Athletes' is the crescent of the circle outside the triangle.
rules.incorrect: Including the intersection region.

rules.title: Two-Set Union Calculation Rule
rules.explanation: To find the number of people belonging to at least one of two groups: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. People belonging to 'Neither' = $\text{Total} - n(A \cup B)$.
rules.correct: In a group of 50: 30 like tea, 25 like coffee, 10 like both. Neither = 50 - (30 + 25 - 10) = 50 - 45 = 5.
rules.incorrect: Subtracting 30 + 25 directly from 50 (yielding negative number).

rules.title: Cross-Professional Compatibility Check
rules.explanation: When evaluating entities like 'Doctors, Engineers, Writers, Women': Ask 'Can a Woman be a Doctor?' (Yes). 'Can a Doctor be a Writer?' (Yes). If all pairs can coexist, use three mutually intersecting circles.
rules.correct: Men, Doctors, Authors: Three partially overlapping circles with a common central triple intersection.
rules.incorrect: Drawing them as isolated circles.

common_mistakes.mistake: Drawing partially overlapping circles for concentric hierarchical categories.
common_mistakes.correction: Biological/geographical subsets (e.g., India, Asia, Earth) are nested concentric circles, not overlapping.
common_mistakes.rationale: Every Indian is an Asian, so the entire India circle must sit inside Asia.

common_mistakes.mistake: Double counting the central triple intersection in demographic surveys.
common_mistakes.correction: Use $n(A \cup B \cup C) = \sum n(A) - \sum n(A \cap B) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$.
common_mistakes.rationale: The triple overlap is subtracted three times in pairwise subtractions, so it must be added back once.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing 'Doctors who are Teachers' with 'ONLY Doctors who are Teachers'.
common_mistakes.correction: 'Doctors who are Teachers' includes those who might also be Rural, unless 'Only' or 'Neither' is stated.
common_mistakes.rationale: Failure to notice the omission of 'Only' leads to picking the wrong numerical region.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming all animals can be pets.
common_mistakes.correction: Pet overlaps with Dog and Cat, but is completely disjoint from Wild animals like Tiger.
common_mistakes.rationale: Realistic taxonomical classification.

quick_revision_points: Concentric circles = Subsets (India in Asia in World)
Disjoint circles = Mutually exclusive categories (Doctor, Lawyer, Engineer)
3 partially overlapping circles = Entities with mutual compatibility (Women, Teachers, Authors)
Two sets: n(A or B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A and B)
Neither = Total - n(A or B)
In geometric diagrams: 'Only' means strictly inside one shape, outside all others
'Both A and B' means the intersection of shapes A and B

lessons.title: Statement and Conclusion: Critical Inferences, Formal Deductions & Argument Validity

content_json.definition: Statement and Conclusion evaluates verbal critical reasoning where candidates determine whether a proposed conclusion is an inevitable, direct logical consequence of a given premise, or an unwarranted assumption. Prominent in SSC CGL Tier 1/2, IBPS PO, RRB NTPC, and State PSCs, problems demand strict factual adherence to the text, elimination of extreme qualifiers ('always', 'never', 'only'), and distinguishing direct inferences from probabilistic opinions.
content_json.overview:
Fundamental Principles of Critical Deduction:
- The Absolute Text Boundary: Accept the statement as 100% indisputable truth; no external real-world knowledge may override the stated facts
- Direct Implication vs Independent Assumption: A valid conclusion is an inevitable result of the statement; an assumption is an unstated prerequisite
- Impact of Extreme Words: Conclusions containing extreme absolutist words ('only', 'all', 'never', 'always', 'everyone') are generally invalid unless the statement explicitly uses identical absolute terms
- Moderate Expressions: Conclusions containing moderate qualifiers ('many', 'some', 'often', 'can', 'likely') are more likely to be logically sustainable
- Cause-and-Effect Alignment: Conclusions suggesting an action must directly correlate with the stated dilemma without introducing extraneous external variables

types.name: 1. Direct Factual Inferences
types.desc: Conclusions that logically restate or directly synthesize the provided empirical data.
examples: Statement: 'Only students who score above 90% receive scholarship. Anita received a scholarship.' Conclusion: 'Anita scored above 90%.' (Valid / Follows)
Statement: 'Most employees take the bus.' Conclusion: 'All employees take public transport.' (Invalid / Does not follow)

types.name: 2. Conditional & If-Then Deductions
types.desc: Evaluating hypothetical scenarios based on causal prerequisites.
examples: Statement: 'If it rains, the cricket match is postponed. Today it rained.' Conclusion: 'The match was postponed.' (Valid)

types.name: 3. Extreme Qualifier Trap Analysis
types.desc: Testing whether absolutist terms distort a generalized or probabilistic statement.
examples: Statement: 'Morning walks improve physical stamina.' Conclusion: 'Only morning walks can improve stamina.' (Invalid due to 'Only')

types.name: 4. Comparative & Superlative Deductions
types.desc: Validating comparisons between entities when baseline criteria are or are not given.
examples: Statement: 'Company A increased its revenue by 15% this quarter.' Conclusion: 'Company A is the most profitable company in the sector.' (Invalid superlative)

types.name: 5. Policy & Governance Cause-Effect
types.desc: Evaluating policy decisions and their direct logical impacts.
examples: Statement: 'Electric vehicle adoption reduces urban particulate emissions.' Conclusion: 'Replacing petrol vehicles with electric reduces urban pollution.' (Valid)

rules.title: Strict Textual Boundary Rule
rules.explanation: Do not bring in outside general knowledge. Even if a conclusion is scientifically or historically true in the real world, if it CANNOT be directly deduced from the given statement, it DOES NOT FOLLOW.
rules.correct: Statement: 'The moon is made of green cheese.' Conclusion: 'The moon is cheese.' (Follows, based strictly on statement).
rules.incorrect: Rejecting the conclusion because the moon is rock in real science.

rules.title: Extreme Qualifier Disqualification Rule
rules.explanation: Conclusions featuring extreme words like 'only', 'all', 'never', 'always', 'completely', 'best', 'sole' almost NEVER follow from a general statement, unless the statement itself uses that exact extreme term.
rules.correct: Statement: 'Many people enjoy coffee.' Conclusion: 'Everyone enjoys coffee.' (Does NOT follow due to 'Everyone').
rules.incorrect: Accepting 'everyone' when the statement only said 'many'.

rules.title: Moderate Words Feasibility Rule
rules.explanation: Conclusions phrased with moderate words like 'some', 'many', 'often', 'can be', 'may' have a high probability of following if they capture the essence of the premise without over-generalizing.
rules.correct: Statement: 'Regular exercise reduces cardiovascular risk.' Conclusion: 'Some individuals who exercise regularly experience reduced cardiac risk.' (Follows).
rules.incorrect: Rejecting moderate conclusions.

rules.title: One-Way Implication Non-Reversibility Rule
rules.explanation: If statement asserts $P \implies Q$, it does NOT mean $Q \implies P$. (e.g., 'All doctors study medicine' does not mean 'Everyone who studies medicine is a doctor').
words: P implies Q != Q implies P
rules.correct: Statement: 'Severe storms cause power outages.' Outage occurs. Conclusion: 'A severe storm must have occurred.' (Does NOT follow: outage could have other causes).
rules.incorrect: Assuming reverse causation.

rules.title: Assumption vs Conclusion Separation Rule
rules.explanation: A conclusion comes AFTER the statement (a consequence or deduction). An assumption comes BEFORE the statement (a presupposition that prompted the speaker). Do not confuse an assumption with a conclusion.
rules.correct: Identifying that a valid conclusion must flow downward from the premise.
rules.incorrect: Selecting a background presupposition as a conclusion.

common_mistakes.mistake: Importing outside general knowledge or personal moral opinions.
common_mistakes.correction: Evaluate conclusions strictly within the four corners of the provided text.
common_mistakes.rationale: Examiners specifically design statements that challenge intuitive real-world assumptions.

common_mistakes.mistake: Accepting conclusions with extreme words like 'only' or 'always'.
common_mistakes.correction: Watch for words like 'only', 'all', 'never'. They immediately flag an over-generalized conclusion.
common_mistakes.rationale: Extreme words are the single most reliable marker of an invalid inference.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating a probable possibility as an inevitable definite conclusion.
common_mistakes.correction: A conclusion must be 100% inevitable. If it 'might' be true but isn't guaranteed, it does not follow.
common_mistakes.rationale: Competitive tests demand definite logical consequence.

common_mistakes.mistake: Committing the converse error ($P \implies Q \implies Q \implies P$).
common_mistakes.correction: Remember that effect does not guarantee one specific cause if alternatives exist.
common_mistakes.rationale: Classic formal logic fallacy.

quick_revision_points: Stick strictly to the statement: zero outside knowledge allowed
Extreme words ('only', 'all', 'never', 'always') almost always make a conclusion invalid
Moderate words ('some', 'often', 'can be') usually signal valid conclusions
P implies Q does NOT mean Q implies P (do not commit converse error)
A conclusion must be 100% inevitable, not just a plausible possibility
Never assume causality where only correlation is mentioned
Distinguish: Assumption comes before statement; Conclusion follows after statement

lessons.title: Puzzles: Multi-Floor Buildings, Box Stacking, Scheduling & Attribute Matrices

content_json.definition: Puzzles in reasoning assess the ability to cross-tabulate complex, unstructured conditions across multiple discrete entities (people, floors, professions, cities, colors, months) into unified consistent grid matrices. A dominant component of Bank PO/Clerk (Mains), SSC CGL Tier 2, and CAT, puzzle solving demands systematic case branching (Case 1 vs Case 2), negative constraint filtering, floor-based vertical numbering (Ground floor = 1 to top floor = N), and week/month scheduling.
content_json.overview:
Fundamental Puzzle Typologies:
- Floor & Flat Puzzles: Multi-storey building (Floors 1 to 8 numbered bottom-to-top) often paired with Flats (Flat A West of Flat B)
- Box Stacking Puzzles: Stack of 7-9 boxes placed one above another with relative gap constraints ('Three boxes between P and Q')
- Day / Month / Date Scheduling: Events scheduled across days (Monday to Sunday) or months with 30 vs 31 days (January, March, April, etc.)
- Multi-Variable Attribute Matrix: Matching 6-8 people with their home state, favorite color, and profession using tick/cross grids
- Comparison / Height / Weight Puzzles: Chaining descending inequalities ($P > Q > R$)

types.name: 1. Multi-Storey Floor Puzzles
types.desc: Arranging 7-9 people on floors numbered 1 (bottom) to N (top) with parity (even/odd floor) rules.
examples: A lives on an odd-numbered floor above floor 4 (Floors 5 or 7)
Two people live between B and C

types.name: 2. Box Stack Positioning
types.desc: Relative vertical placement of boxes where absolute floor numbers are not predetermined.
examples: Box T is placed immediately above Box R
As many boxes are above P as below Q

types.name: 3. Date & Month Scheduling Puzzles
types.desc: Scheduling seminars or interviews on specific dates (e.g., 7th and 14th) across 4 months.
examples: Months with 30 days (April, June, Sept, Nov) vs 31 days (Jan, March, May, July, Aug, Oct, Dec)
Person attends seminar in a month having 30 days

types.name: 4. Matrix / Cross-Tabulation Puzzles
types.desc: Matching 3 or 4 attributes per person using systematic elimination tables.
examples: A does not like Red and is not a Doctor
The engineer wears Green and lives in Mumbai

types.name: 5. Order & Ranking Comparison Chains
types.desc: Ranking 6 individuals by weight or salary with partial inequality clues.
examples: Only two persons are heavier than M (M is 3rd from top in descending order)

rules.title: Dual-Case Branching Method
