lessons.title: Physics: Mechanics, Newton's Laws, Gravitation, Thermodynamics, Optics & Electricity

content_json.definition: Physics in competitive examinations (UPSC CSE, SSC CGL/CHSL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC/JE, CDS, NDA, State PSCs) investigates the fundamental physical laws governing matter, energy, space, and time. Core areas include classical mechanics, kinematics, gravitation, fluid statics and dynamics, heat and thermodynamics, wave mechanics, geometrical and physical optics, electrostatics, electromagnetism, and atomic-nuclear physics.
content_json.overview:
Comprehensive Physical Principles Framework:
- Mechanics & Dynamics: Scalar vs Vector quantities; Newton's Three Laws of Motion ($F = ma$, Action-Reaction); Conservation of Linear Momentum; Work ($W = F d \cos\theta$), Kinetic Energy ($E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$), Potential Energy ($E_p = mgh$); Power ($P = W/t$ in Watts)
- Gravitation & Planetary Motion: Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation ($F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$); Acceleration due to gravity ($g \approx 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, varies from minimum at equator to maximum at poles, zero at Earth center); Escape Velocity ($v_e = \sqrt{2gR} \approx 11.2\text{ km/s}$ for Earth); Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion
- Properties of Matter & Fluids: Hooke's Law; Pascal's Principle (hydraulic press); Archimedes' Principle (buoyancy, law of floatation); Bernoulli's Principle (aerodynamic lift, venturimeter); Surface Tension (capillarity, spherical water drops); Viscosity (Poiseuille's flow)
- Heat & Thermodynamics: Temperature scales ($C/5 = (F-32)/9 = (K-273)/5$); Anomalous expansion of water ($4^\circ\text{C}$ maximum density); Triple point of water ($273.16\text{ K}$); Laws of Thermodynamics (Zeroth law defines temperature, First law defines internal energy conservation $\Delta Q = \Delta U + W$, Second law defines entropy and impossibility of perpetual motion machine of second kind)
- Waves, Sound & Acoustics: Transverse vs Longitudinal waves; Audible sound ($20\text{ Hz} - 20,000\text{ Hz}$), Infrasonic ($<20\text{ Hz}$), Ultrasonic ($>20,000\text{ Hz}$, SONAR, bat echolocation); Speed of sound is fastest in solids, slower in liquids, slowest in gases, zero in vacuum; Doppler Effect
- Optics & Light: Speed of light in vacuum ($c = 3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}$); Laws of Reflection ($i = r$); Refraction (Snell's Law $n_1\sin i = n_2\sin r$); Total Internal Reflection (optical fibres, mirage, diamond brilliance; condition: denser to rarer medium and $i > \theta_c$); Dispersion (rainbow); Scattering (Rayleigh scattering $\propto 1/\lambda^4$, blue sky, red sunset); Human eye defects (Myopia corrected by concave lens, Hypermetropia corrected by convex lens, Presbyopia by bifocal lens)
- Electricity & Magnetism: Coulomb's Law; Ohm's Law ($V = IR$); Electric Power ($P = VI = I^2R = V^2/R$, $1\text{ kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6\text{ J}$); Resistors in series ($R = R_1 + R_2$) vs parallel ($1/R = 1/R_1 + 1/R_2$); Fleming's Left-Hand Rule (electric motors) and Right-Hand Rule (electric generators); Faraday's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction; Transformer (mutual induction, works on AC only)
- Modern Physics: Photoelectric Effect ($E = h\nu$, Einstein 1905 Nobel Prize 1921); Radioactivity (Becquerel, Curie; alpha, beta, gamma rays); Nuclear Fission (U-235, nuclear power plants, atomic bombs) vs Nuclear Fusion (Hydrogen bomb, Sun's energy generation via proton-proton chain)

types.name: 1. Classical Mechanics & Kinematics
types.desc: Fundamental laws of motion, force systems, energy conservation, and gravitation.
examples: Newton's 1st Law (Inertia) • Newton's 2nd Law (F = ma) • Newton's 3rd Law (Action = Reaction)
Escape velocity from Earth surface = 11.2 km/s • g value is maximum at poles and zero at Earth's center

types.name: 2. Fluid Mechanics & Atmospheric Physics
types.desc: Pressure distributions, buoyancy, surface tension, and aerodynamic lift.
examples: Archimedes' Principle: Floating body displaces liquid equal to its own weight
Bernoulli's Theorem: Explains dynamic lift in airplanes and spinning ball curve
Surface Tension: Spherical shape of rain drops and oil spreading on water

types.name: 3. Thermal Physics & Thermodynamics
types.desc: Heat transfer mechanisms, anomalous expansion, and thermodynamic laws.
examples: Conduction (solids) • Convection (fluids) • Radiation (vacuum via electromagnetic waves)
Anomalous expansion of water: Density is maximum and volume is minimum at 4°C

types.name: 4. Wave Optics, Sound & Acoustics
types.desc: Wave propagation, acoustic frequencies, reflection, refraction, and optical phenomena.
examples: Total Internal Reflection (TIR): Optical fibers, mirages in deserts, sparkling diamonds
Scattering of Light: Blue color of sky due to Rayleigh scattering (Intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴)
Ultrasonic waves (>20 kHz) used in SONAR and medical ultrasonography

types.name: 5. Electricity, Electromagnetism & Modern Physics
types.desc: Circuits, magnetic effects of current, induction, and nuclear reactions.
examples: Ohm's Law: V = IR • 1 kWh commercial unit of electricity = 3.6 × 10⁶ Joules
Transformers operate strictly on Alternating Current (AC) via Mutual Induction
Nuclear Fusion: Source of stellar energy in the Sun (conversion of Hydrogen into Helium)

rules.title: Variation of Acceleration Due to Gravity (g) Rule
rules.explanation: Acceleration due to gravity ($g = GM/R^2$) is NOT constant over Earth's surface. Because Earth is an oblate spheroid, $R$ is smaller at the poles and larger at the equator: $g_{\text{poles}} > g_{\text{equator}}$. Moreover, $g$ decreases with both altitude ($h$) and depth ($d$), becoming exactly ZERO at the center of the Earth.
rules.correct: A person weighs maximum at the North/South poles and minimum at the equator; weight becomes zero at the center of the Earth.
rules.incorrect: A body weighs the same everywhere on Earth, or weight is maximum at the equator.

rules.title: Total Internal Reflection (TIR) Conditions Rule
rules.explanation: TIR occurs ONLY when two strict conditions are met: (1) Light must travel from an optically denser medium to an optically rarer medium (e.g., glass to air, water to air); and (2) The angle of incidence ($i$) must exceed the critical angle ($\theta_c$) for that pair of media.
rules.correct: Optical fibers transmit data with near-zero loss using Total Internal Reflection as light moves inside the denser core.
rules.incorrect: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from air into water (rarer to denser).

rules.title: Speed of Sound Medium Dependency Rule
rules.explanation: Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave requiring a material medium for propagation. It CANNOT travel through vacuum. The velocity of sound depends on the medium's elasticity and density: $v_{\text{solids}} > v_{\text{liquids}} > v_{\text{gases}}$. Speed of sound in steel is $\approx 5100\text{ m/s}$, in water $\approx 1480\text{ m/s}$, and in dry air at $20^\circ\text{C}$ is $\approx 343\text{ m/s}$.
rules.correct: Sound travels faster in steel (solid) than in water (liquid) and cannot propagate in a vacuum.
rules.incorrect: Sound travels faster in air than in steel, or sound can propagate through vacuum.

rules.title: Eye Vision Defects & Lens Correction Rule
rules.explanation: Myopia (Short-sightedness): Distant objects appear blurry because image forms in front of the retina; corrected using a CONCAVE (diverging) lens. Hypermetropia (Long-sightedness): Near objects appear blurry because image forms behind the retina; corrected using a CONVEX (converging) lens.
rules.correct: Myopia is corrected by using a concave lens of appropriate focal length.
rules.incorrect: Myopia is corrected by wearing convex spectacles (convex lenses correct hypermetropia).

rules.title: Nuclear Energy: Fission vs. Fusion Distinction Rule
rules.explanation: Nuclear Fission: Heavy unstable nucleus (like Uranium-235 or Plutonium-239) splits into lighter nuclei with release of neutrons and energy (used in commercial Nuclear Reactors and Atomic Bombs). Nuclear Fusion: Light nuclei (Hydrogen isotopes like Deuterium and Tritium) combine at extremely high temperatures to form a heavier nucleus like Helium (source of energy in the Sun, stars, and Hydrogen Bombs).
rules.correct: The energy radiated by the Sun and stars is generated by thermonuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium.
rules.incorrect: Solar energy is generated by nuclear fission of uranium in the solar core.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing that mass of an object changes when taken to the Moon.
common_mistakes.correction: Mass ($m$) is an invariant scalar quantity and remains constant everywhere in the universe. Only Weight ($W = mg$) changes because Moon's gravity is 1/6th of Earth's gravity.
common_mistakes.rationale: Candidates frequently confuse the fundamental quantity mass (kg) with the force weight (Newtons).

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking that a transformer can be used to step up Direct Current (DC) voltage.
common_mistakes.correction: Transformers operate strictly on the principle of Mutual Induction, which requires a continuously changing magnetic flux produced only by Alternating Current (AC). In DC, flux is constant, so induced EMF is zero.
common_mistakes.rationale: Exam questions test the core working principle of electrical transformers.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming sound travels faster in dry air than in humid air.
common_mistakes.correction: Sound travels faster in humid air than in dry air because humid air contains water vapor, which reduces the effective molecular mass of air, thereby reducing density and increasing acoustic velocity ($v \propto 1/\sqrt{\rho}$).
common_mistakes.rationale: Density of water vapor ($18\text{ g/mol}$) is less than dry air ($pprox 29\text{ g/mol}$).

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing the color of sky at sunset with dispersion instead of scattering.
common_mistakes.correction: The red/orange sky during sunset and sunrise is caused by Rayleigh scattering of light, where shorter blue wavelengths are scattered away over the long atmospheric path, leaving longer red wavelengths to reach our eyes.
common_mistakes.rationale: Dispersion splits white light into a spectrum via prism/raindrop, while scattering redirects wavelengths according to particle size.

quick_revision_points: SI Fundamental Units: Length (m), Mass (kg), Time (s), Electric Current (A), Temperature (K), Amount of Substance (mol), Luminous Intensity (cd).
Derived Units: Force = Newton (N = kg·m/s²), Work/Energy = Joule (J = N·m), Power = Watt (W = J/s), Pressure = Pascal (Pa = N/m²), Frequency = Hertz (Hz = 1/s).
1 Horsepower (HP) = 746 Watts | 1 Commercial Unit of Electricity (1 kWh) = 3.6 × 10⁶ Joules.
Acceleration due to gravity: g ≈ 9.8 m/s² on Earth; g_moon ≈ g_earth / 6. Value of g is maximum at poles, minimum at equator, zero at center of Earth.
Escape Velocity: From Earth = 11.2 km/s; From Moon = 2.4 km/s (explaining why Moon has no atmosphere).
Anomalous Expansion of Water: Water attains maximum density and minimum volume at 4°C (enabling aquatic life survival under frozen lakes).
Speed of Light: In vacuum c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s; In water = 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s; In glass = 2 × 10⁸ m/s. Refractive index n = c/v.
Total Internal Reflection (TIR): Requires light moving from denser to rarer medium and angle of incidence > critical angle. Explains optical fibers, mirages, and diamond sparkle.
Scattering of Light: Rayleigh Scattering Intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴. Shorter blue wavelengths scatter most (blue sky), longer red wavelengths penetrate dust/fog (danger signals are red).
Human Eye: Least distance of distinct vision = 25 cm. Myopia (nearsightedness) corrected by concave lens; Hypermetropia (farsightedness) corrected by convex lens.
Electric Circuit Laws: Ohm's Law V = IR. In series, Current (I) remains constant; in parallel, Voltage (V) remains constant.
Transformers: Operate exclusively on AC through mutual induction. Step-up transformer increases voltage, step-down decreases voltage.
Nuclear Physics: Nuclear Fission powers nuclear reactors (U-235, controlled chain reaction with cadmium control rods and heavy water/graphite moderator). Nuclear Fusion powers the Sun.

lessons.title: Chemistry: Atomic Structure, Periodic Table Trends, Chemical Bonding, Acids, Bases, Salts, Metallurgy & Everyday Polymers

content_json.definition: Chemistry in competitive examinations (UPSC, SSC CGL/CHSL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC/JE, CDS, State PSCs) examines the composition, structure, properties, and reactions of matter. The syllabus encompasses fundamental atomic models, modern periodic table classifications and periodic trends, chemical bonding, acid-base-salt equilibria and pH scales, extraction of metals and metallurgy, alloys, electrochemistry, and organic chemistry applications including polymers, soaps, detergents, fuels, and daily household compounds.
content_json.overview:
Comprehensive Chemical Science Framework:
- Atomic Structure & Models: Subatomic particles (Electron discovered by J.J. Thomson, Proton by E. Goldstein/Rutherford, Neutron by James Chadwick 1932); Thomson's Plum Pudding Model; Rutherford's Alpha Scattering Experiment (discovery of dense positive nucleus); Bohr's Model (quantized energy levels); Quantum numbers; Isotopes (same atomic number $Z$, different mass number $A$, e.g., Protium, Deuterium, Tritium), Isobars (same $A$, different $Z$), Isotones (same number of neutrons)
- Modern Periodic Table & Trends: Moseley's Modern Periodic Law (properties are periodic functions of atomic numbers); 7 Periods and 18 Groups; Periodic Trends: Atomic radius decreases across a period (left to right) and increases down a group; Ionization energy and Electronegativity increase across a period and decrease down a group; Fluorine is the most electronegative element; Francium/Cesium are the most electropositive
- Chemical Bonding: Ionic/Electrovalent bond (complete electron transfer, high melting/boiling points, conduct in molten/aqueous states); Covalent bond (electron sharing); Coordinate/Dative bond; Hydrogen bonding (explains high boiling point of water and double helix structure of DNA)
- Acids, Bases & Salts: Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, and Lewis concepts; pH scale ($0-14$, Sorenson 1909; $\text{pH} = -\log_{10}[\text{H}^+]$); Universal and natural indicators (Litmus turns red in acid and blue in base; Phenolphthalein is colorless in acid and pink in base; Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in base); Common salts: Baking Soda ($\text{NaHCO}_3$, Sodium hydrogen carbonate), Washing Soda ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3\cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$), Bleaching Powder ($\text{CaOCl}_2$, Calcium hypochlorite), Plaster of Paris ($\text{CaSO}_4\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$), Gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_4\cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$)
- Metals, Non-Metals & Metallurgy: Reactivity series of metals (K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au); Ores (Bauxite for Aluminium, Haematite/Magnetite for Iron, Cinnabar for Mercury, Galena for Lead); Extraction processes (Roasting, Calcination, Smelting); Important Alloys (Brass = $\text{Cu} + \text{Zn}$; Bronze = $\text{Cu} + \text{Sn}$; Solder = $\text{Pb} + \text{Sn}$; Stainless Steel = $\text{Fe} + \text{Cr} + \text{Ni} + \text{C}$; German Silver = $\text{Cu} + \text{Zn} + \text{Ni}$ containing NO silver!)
- Electrochemistry & Corrosion: Galvanic/Voltaic cell; Rusting of iron ($2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3\cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$, requires both oxygen and water); Prevention: Galvanization (coating iron with Zinc); Cathodic protection
- Organic Chemistry & Daily Materials: Hydrocarbons (Alkanes $C_n H_{2n+2}$, Alkenes $C_n H_{2n}$, Alkynes $C_n H_{2n-2}$, Aromatic Benzene $C_6H_6$); Commercial fuels (LPG mainly Butane + Propane with Ethyl Mercaptan odorant; CNG mainly Methane $\text{CH}_4$); Polymers: Natural (cellulose, natural rubber with isoprene monomer) vs Synthetic (Polythene, PVC, Teflon / PTFE, Nylon 6,6, Bakelite, Rayon / artificial silk); Soaps (sodium/potassium salts of fatty acids) vs Detergents (cleans in hard water containing $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ ions)

types.name: 1. Atomic Structure & Subatomic Particles
types.desc: Particle discoveries, nuclear structure, electron configurations, and isotopes.
examples: Electron (J.J. Thomson) • Proton (Goldstein/Rutherford) • Neutron (James Chadwick 1932)
Isotopes of Hydrogen: Protium (¹H), Deuterium (²H - heavy water D₂O), Tritium (³H - radioactive)

types.name: 2. Modern Periodic Table & Periodic Trends
types.desc: Arrangement by atomic number (Moseley) and systematic property trends.
examples: Electronegativity: Maximum in Fluorine (F), minimum in Francium/Cesium
Atomic Radius: Decreases across a period (left to right), increases down a group
Noble Gases (Group 18): Chemically inert full valence shell (Helium, Neon, Argon, Radon)

types.name: 3. Acids, Bases, Salts & pH Chemistry
types.desc: pH scale, neutralization, chemical indicators, and commercial inorganic salts.
examples: Baking Soda (NaHCO₃) • Washing Soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) • Bleaching Powder (CaOCl₂)
Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O) prepared by heating Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) at 373 K
Acid Rain: Rainwater with pH < 5.6 caused by SO₂ and NO₂ atmospheric emissions

types.name: 4. Metallurgy, Ores & Commercial Alloys
types.desc: Metal extraction, reactivity series, and widely used industrial alloys.
examples: Brass: Copper + Zinc • Bronze: Copper + Tin • Solder: Lead + Tin
German Silver: Copper + Zinc + Nickel (Note: Contains 0% Silver!)
Galvanization: Coating steel or iron with a sacrificial layer of Zinc to prevent rust

types.name: 5. Organic Compounds, Fuels & Daily Polymers
types.desc: Hydrocarbons, cooking gases, thermosetting plastics, and detergents.
examples: LPG (Liquefied Petroleum Gas): Primarily Butane and Propane with Ethyl Mercaptan odorant
CNG (Compressed Natural Gas): Primarily Methane (CH₄, 85-90%)
Teflon (PTFE): Non-stick cookware coating • Bakelite: Electrical switches (thermosetting)

rules.title: Modern Periodic Law & Atomic Number Basis Rule
rules.explanation: Mendeleev organized elements by Atomic Mass, leading to anomalies. Henry Moseley (1913) formulated the Modern Periodic Law: properties of elements are periodic functions of their ATOMIC NUMBER (nuclear charge Z). This placed elements strictly by electronic configuration into 7 periods and 18 groups.
rules.correct: The Modern Periodic Table is arranged in increasing order of atomic numbers, not atomic masses.
rules.incorrect: The modern periodic table is classified on the basis of increasing atomic masses.

rules.title: Periodic Table Trends Directionality Rule
rules.explanation: Remember the diagonal trend: Ionization Energy, Electron Affinity, and Electronegativity INCREASE from bottom-left to top-right (Fluorine is highest). Conversely, Atomic Radius and Metallic Character INCREASE from top-right to bottom-left (Cesium/Francium is largest and most metallic).
rules.correct: Across a period from left to right, electronegativity increases and atomic size decreases.
rules.incorrect: Atomic radius increases across a period from left to right.

rules.title: Gypsum to Plaster of Paris Dehydration Rule
rules.explanation: Gypsum is Calcium Sulphate Dihydrate ($CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O$). When carefully heated to $373\text{ K}$ ($100^\circ\text{C}$), it loses three-fourths of its water of crystallization to form Plaster of Paris (POP, Calcium Sulphate Hemihydrate $CaSO_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}H_2O$). When mixed with water, POP sets into a hard solid mass by reverting to Gypsum.
rules.correct: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate ($CaSO_4 \cdot 0.5H_2O$).
rules.incorrect: Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate dihydrate ($CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O$).

rules.title: Alloy Composition Disambiguation Rule
rules.explanation: Brass = Copper ($70\%$) + Zinc ($30\%$); Bronze = Copper ($90\%$) + Tin ($10\%$); German Silver = Copper + Zinc + Nickel (contains ZERO percent silver!); Solder = Lead + Tin (low melting point for electronics).
rules.correct: German Silver is an alloy composed of Copper, Zinc, and Nickel with no silver present.
rules.incorrect: German Silver contains 25% elemental silver.

rules.title: LPG Odorant & Fuel Composition Rule
rules.explanation: Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) consists mainly of butane and propane, which are naturally odorless. To detect dangerous gas leaks, a foul-smelling sulfur compound called Ethyl Mercaptan ($C_2H_5SH$) is deliberately added.
rules.correct: Ethyl mercaptan is added to domestic LPG cylinders to provide a strong detectable odor for leak detection.
rules.incorrect: Pure butane has a naturally pungent rotting smell.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking 'German Silver' contains silver.
common_mistakes.correction: German Silver contains Copper (50%), Zinc (30%), and Nickel (20%). It is named solely for its silvery appearance and contains 0% silver.
common_mistakes.rationale: Examiners routinely include 'Silver' in MCQ options to trap unwary candidates.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing Baking Soda with Washing Soda formulas.
common_mistakes.correction: Baking Soda is Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate ($NaHCO_3$), while Washing Soda is Sodium Carbonate Decahydrate ($Na_2CO_3 \cdot 10H_2O$).
common_mistakes.rationale: Both are sodium carbonate salts, but baking soda contains hydrogen ('bi-carbonate').

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming rust formation requires only oxygen.
common_mistakes.correction: Rusting of iron requires BOTH oxygen ($O_2$) and moisture/water ($H_2O$). In dry air or air-free boiled water, iron does not rust.
common_mistakes.rationale: Rusting is an electrochemical corrosion process needing both oxidizing agent and electrolytic medium.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing hard water can be effectively cleaned using ordinary soap.
common_mistakes.correction: Ordinary soaps react with $Ca^{2+}$ and $Mg^{2+}$ ions in hard water to form an insoluble white precipitate called 'scum', wasting soap. Synthetic detergents do not form scum and clean efficiently in hard water.
common_mistakes.rationale: Soaps form insoluble calcium and magnesium stearates, whereas alkyl benzene sulfonates in detergents remain soluble.

quick_revision_points: Atomic Particles: Electron (J.J. Thomson), Proton (E. Goldstein/Rutherford), Neutron (James Chadwick 1932).
Atomic Number (Z) = Number of protons in nucleus. Mass Number (A) = Protons + Neutrons.
Modern Periodic Law (Moseley 1913): Elements are arranged in 7 periods and 18 groups by increasing atomic number.
Periodic Trends: Electronegativity and Ionization Energy increase from left to right; Atomic Radius increases from top to bottom.
Most Electronegative element = Fluorine (F). Most Electropositive element = Cesium (Cs) / Francium (Fr).
pH Scale: Acidic < 7, Neutral = 7 (pure water at 25°C), Basic > 7. Human blood pH is strictly maintained around 7.35 - 7.45.
Litmus Indicator: Red in acidic solution, Blue in basic solution. Phenolphthalein: Colorless in acid, Pink in base.
Baking Soda = Sodium Bicarbonate (NaHCO₃). Washing Soda = Sodium Carbonate Decahydrate (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O).
Bleaching Powder = Calcium Hypochlorite (CaOCl₂). Quicklime = CaO. Slaked Lime = Ca(OH)₂.
Plaster of Paris (POP) = CaSO₄·½H₂O (Calcium sulphate hemihydrate), prepared by heating Gypsum (CaSO₄·2H₂O) to 373 K.
Key Alloys: Brass (Cu + Zn), Bronze (Cu + Sn), German Silver (Cu + Zn + Ni, NO silver), Solder (Pb + Sn), Amalgam (alloy with Mercury).
Galvanization: Coating iron or steel with a protective layer of Zinc to prevent rusting.
LPG = Liquefied Petroleum Gas (Butane + Propane; Ethyl Mercaptan odorant added for leak detection). CNG = Compressed Natural Gas (mainly Methane CH₄).
Polymers: Teflon (Polytetrafluoroethylene - non-stick cookware), Bakelite (thermosetting plastic - electrical switches), PVC (polyvinyl chloride - pipes).

lessons.title: Biology: Cell Biology, Whittaker's Five Kingdoms, Plant Physiology, Genetics & Evolution

content_json.definition: Biology in competitive examinations (UPSC, SSC CGL/CHSL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC, State PSCs, CDS, NDA) examines living systems, cellular architecture, taxonomy and biological diversity, plant metabolic physiology, molecular genetics, and mechanisms of inheritance and evolutionary adaptation.
content_json.overview:
Comprehensive Biological Sciences Framework:
- Cell Biology (Cytology): Cell Theory (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow); Prokaryotic vs Eukaryotic cells; Cell Organelles: Nucleus (brain of the cell, contains chromatin & nucleolus), Mitochondria ('Powerhouse of the cell', site of ATP synthesis via Krebs cycle), Chloroplasts ('Kitchen of the cell', site of photosynthesis in plants), Ribosomes ('Protein factories', site of translation, non-membrane bound), Endoplasmic Reticulum (Rough ER with ribosomes synthesizes proteins, Smooth ER synthesizes lipids and detoxifies drugs), Golgi Apparatus (packaging and secretional dispatch), Lysosomes ('Suicide bags' with hydrolytic enzymes), Vacuoles; Cell division: Mitosis (equational division, somatic growth, 2 diploid daughter cells) vs Meiosis (reductional division, gametogenesis, 4 haploid daughter cells, crossing over in Pachytene)
- Biological Taxonomy & Classification: Carl Linnaeus (Father of Taxonomy, Binomial Nomenclature: *Genus species*); R.H. Whittaker's 5-Kingdom Classification (1969): Monera (unicellular prokaryotes like bacteria, cyanobacteria), Protista (unicellular eukaryotes like Amoeba, Paramecium, Plasmodium), Fungi (heterotrophic, chitinous cell walls, saprophytic molds/mushrooms), Plantae (autotrophic, cellulose cell walls), Animalia (heterotrophic, no cell walls); Plant Kingdom divisions: Thallophyta (algae), Bryophyta (amphibians of plant kingdom, e.g., moss, Riccia), Pteridophyta (ferns, first vascular plants), Gymnosperms (naked seeds, e.g., Cycas, Pinus), Angiosperms (flowering plants with enclosed seeds in fruit)
- Plant Physiology & Transport: Xylem (conducts water and minerals upward via transpiration pull; dead tracheids and vessels) vs Phloem (translocates organic food bidirectionally; living sieve tubes and companion cells); Photosynthesis ($6\text{CO}_2 + 12\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{Light, Chlorophyll}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} + 6\text{O}_2$; Light reaction in thylakoid grana releasing $\text{O}_2$ from photolysis of water; Dark/Calvin cycle in stroma fixing $\text{CO}_2$); Plant Hormones: Auxins (apical dominance, phototropism, discovered by Went), Gibberellins (stem elongation, seed germination), Cytokinins (cell division, delay senescence), Abscisic Acid (ABA, 'stress hormone', causes stomatal closure and leaf abscission), Ethylene (only gaseous plant hormone, promotes fruit ripening)
- Genetics & Molecular Biology: Gregor Johann Mendel (Father of Genetics, experiments on garden pea *Pisum sativum*, Laws of Segregation and Independent Assortment); DNA Structure (Watson and Crick 1953 double helix; nitrogenous bases: Adenine pairs with Thymine via 2 H-bonds, Guanine pairs with Cytosine via 3 H-bonds); RNA (Ribose sugar, Uracil replaces Thymine); Central Dogma: $\text{DNA} \xrightarrow{\text{Transcription}} \text{mRNA} \xrightarrow{\text{Translation}} \text{Protein}$; Genetic code is triplet, universal, degenerate; Sex determination in humans (Male XY, Female XX; Y chromosome determines male sex); Genetic disorders (Down syndrome: Trisomy 21; Turner syndrome: 45,XO; Klinefelter syndrome: 47,XXY; Hemophilia & Color Blindness: X-linked recessive)

types.name: 1. Cytology & Cell Organelles
types.desc: Cell theory, ultrastructure of plant/animal cells, and specialized organelle functions.
examples: Mitochondria: Powerhouse of the cell (produces ATP through cellular respiration)
Lysosomes: Suicidal bags (contain acid hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion)
Ribosomes: Protein factories of the cell (found free or bound to Rough ER)

types.name: 2. Whittaker's 5 Kingdoms & Taxonomy
types.desc: Classification of living organisms based on cell structure, body organization, and nutrition.
examples: Monera (Bacteria, prokaryotic) • Protista (Amoeba, eukaryotic unicellular)
Fungi (Molds, mushrooms, chitin wall) • Plantae (Autotrophic) • Animalia (Heterotrophic)

types.name: 3. Plant Tissues & Vascular Transport
types.desc: Complex permanent tissues responsible for conduction of water, minerals, and nutrients.
examples: Xylem: Transports water and inorganic minerals unidirectionally from roots to leaves
Phloem: Transports synthesized organic sugars bidirectionally from source to sink

types.name: 4. Photosynthesis & Plant Phytohormones
types.desc: Light-driven energy capture, water photolysis, and growth regulators.
examples: Oxygen released during photosynthesis originates from water (H₂O), NOT from CO₂
Auxins (stem elongation, phototropism) • Ethylene (gaseous hormone, fruit ripening)

types.name: 5. Mendelian Genetics & Molecular DNA
types.desc: Inheritance laws, double-helix structure, protein synthesis, and chromosomal mutations.
examples: DNA Base Pairing: Adenine = Thymine (2 H-bonds), Guanine ≡ Cytosine (3 H-bonds)
Down Syndrome: Caused by chromosomal non-disjunction resulting in Trisomy 21

rules.title: Origin of Photosynthetic Oxygen Rule
rules.explanation: In green plant photosynthesis, the oxygen gas ($O_2$) released into the atmosphere is derived strictly from the photolysis (light-dependent cleavage) of WATER ($H_2O$), and NOT from carbon dioxide ($CO_2$). Carbon dioxide is reduced to synthesize glucose.
rules.correct: The oxygen liberated during photosynthesis comes from the splitting of water molecules.
rules.incorrect: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from carbon dioxide molecules.

rules.title: Mitochondria & Chloroplast Semi-Autonomous Nature Rule
rules.explanation: Mitochondria and Chloroplasts are semi-autonomous double-membraned organelles that possess their OWN circular DNA and 70S ribosomes. They can synthesize some of their own proteins and replicate independently within the host cell (Endosymbiotic Theory).
rules.correct: Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain their own circular DNA and protein-synthesizing ribosomes.
rules.incorrect: Mitochondria and chloroplasts rely entirely on nuclear DNA and have no genetic material of their own.

rules.title: Plant Phytohormone Functional Specificity Rule
rules.explanation: Auxin promotes apical dominance and causes bending towards light (phototropism); Gibberellins break seed dormancy and cause internode elongation; Cytokinins promote cell division; Abscisic acid (ABA) is a growth inhibitor ('stress hormone' closing stomata); Ethylene is the UNIQUE GASEOUS hormone causing fruit ripening.
rules.correct: Ethylene is the only gaseous phytohormone naturally responsible for ripening of fruits.
rules.incorrect: Auxin is a gaseous hormone used for fruit ripening.

rules.title: Xylem vs. Phloem Directional Transport Rule
rules.explanation: Xylem transports water and dissolved mineral nutrients UNIDIRECTIONALLY from roots upwards to stems and leaves via negative pressure transpiration pull. Phloem translocates dissolved organic solutes (sucrose) BIDIRECTIONALLY from leaves (source) to storage organs or growing buds (sink).
rules.correct: Water transport in xylem is strictly unidirectional (upward), whereas translocation in phloem is bidirectional.
rules.incorrect: Xylem transports organic food bidirectionally, while phloem transports water only downwards.

rules.title: DNA vs. RNA Nitrogenous Base Complementarity Rule
rules.explanation: DNA contains four nitrogenous bases: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), and Cytosine (C). In RNA, THYMINE IS REPLACED BY URACIL (U). Complementary pairing: In DNA, A pairs with T (2 H-bonds) and G with C (3 H-bonds). In RNA, A pairs with U.
rules.correct: RNA contains Uracil in place of Thymine.
rules.incorrect: RNA contains Thymine in place of Uracil, or Guanine is absent in RNA.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking that all plant cells have chloroplasts.
common_mistakes.correction: Chloroplasts are present only in green photosynthetic cells (like leaf mesophyll). Non-green plant cells, such as underground root cells and internal bark cells, do not contain chloroplasts (they contain non-pigmented leucoplasts).
common_mistakes.rationale: Candidates mistakenly generalize green leaf characteristics to every anatomical cell of a plant.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing Mitosis with Meiosis daughter cell chromosome numbers.
common_mistakes.correction: Mitosis produces 2 genetically identical diploid ($2n$) daughter cells. Meiosis produces 4 genetically varied haploid ($n$) daughter cells.
common_mistakes.rationale: Meiosis is a reductional division essential for gamete formation, whereas mitosis is an equational division for growth.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing viruses belong to Whittaker's Monera kingdom.
common_mistakes.correction: Viruses are acellular and non-living outside a host cell. Because they lack cellular structure and metabolic machinery, they are NOT placed in any of Whittaker's 5 kingdoms.
common_mistakes.rationale: Viruses occupy a twilight zone between living and non-living matter and are excluded from cellular classification.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming human male sex is determined by the mother's egg.
common_mistakes.correction: All human female ova carry an X chromosome ($22+X$). Human male sperm cells carry either an X ($22+X$) or a Y ($22+Y$) chromosome in equal proportion (50:50). The father's sperm cell determines the chromosomal sex of the offspring.
common_mistakes.rationale: The presence or absence of the Y chromosome (specifically the SRY gene) determines male testicular development.

quick_revision_points: Cell Theory: Proposed by Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann (1838-39); Rudolf Virchow added 'Omnis cellula e cellula' (all cells arise from pre-existing cells).
Mitochondria: Powerhouse of the cell; produces ATP via cellular respiration. Contains own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes.
Chloroplasts: Kitchen of the cell; site of photosynthesis. Contains green pigment Chlorophyll (which contains Magnesium ion at its center).
Ribosomes: Protein factories; synthesized in nucleolus. Lack membrane; 70S in prokaryotes, 80S in eukaryotes.
Lysosomes: Suicidal bags containing acid hydrolytic enzymes (active at pH ~5.0) that digest foreign pathogens and worn-out organelles.
Whittaker's 5 Kingdoms (1969): Monera (prokaryotes), Protista (unicellular eukaryotes), Fungi (chitin wall), Plantae (cellulose wall), Animalia (no cell wall).
Bryophytes: Known as the 'Amphibians of the Plant Kingdom' because they live in soil but depend on water for sexual reproduction (e.g., Mosses, Marchantia).
Xylem vs Phloem: Xylem conducts water/minerals upward unidirectionally. Phloem translocates sucrose bidirectionally.
Photosynthesis: Oxygen liberated is released by the photolysis of water ($H_2O$), driven by sunlight captured by chlorophyll.
Phytohormones: Auxin (phototropism/apical dominance), Gibberellin (seed germination/stem elongation), Cytokinin (cell division), ABA (stress hormone/stomata closure), Ethylene (fruit ripening gas).
Father of Genetics: Gregor Johann Mendel (worked on garden peas, *Pisum sativum*).
DNA Structure: Discovered by Watson and Crick (1953 double helix). Bases: A pairs with T (2 H-bonds); G pairs with C (3 H-bonds).
RNA: Single-stranded; contains ribose sugar and Uracil (U) instead of Thymine (T).
Human Karyotype: 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 total): 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of allosomes/sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male).

lessons.title: Human Body: Organ Systems, Circulation, Nervous System, Endocrine Hormones, Nutrition & Deficiency Diseases

content_json.definition: Human Anatomy and Physiology in competitive examinations (UPSC, SSC CGL/CHSL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC, State PSCs, CDS, NDA) covers the structure and integrated functioning of human organ systems: circulatory and blood groups, nervous coordination and brain architecture, digestive enzymes, endocrine glands and hormonal homeostasis, respiratory gas exchange, renal excretion, and nutritional vitamins and deficiency disorders.
content_json.overview:
Comprehensive Human Physiology Framework:
- Circulatory System & Blood: Four-chambered heart (2 atria, 2 ventricles); Double circulation (systemic and pulmonary); Pacemaker of heart is SA Node (Sinoatrial node) generating electrical impulses; Blood composition: Plasma ($55\%$), Formed elements ($45\%$ - RBCs/Erythrocytes [contain iron-rich Haemoglobin, lifespan ~120 days, graveyard is Spleen], WBCs/Leukocytes [defense, granular vs agranular], Platelets/Thrombocytes [blood clotting with Prothrombin, Fibrinogen, Calcium and Vitamin K]); Blood Groups (Karl Landsteiner 1900): ABO system (Type O is Universal Donor, Type AB is Universal Recipient); Rh Factor (Rhesus factor, Rh incompatibility causes Erythroblastosis Fetalis in second Rh-positive child of Rh-negative mother)
- Nervous System & Sense Organs: Central Nervous System (Brain and Spinal Cord) vs Peripheral Nervous System; Human Brain: Forebrain (Cerebrum [largest part, seat of intelligence, memory, voluntary actions], Thalamus, Hypothalamus [regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, pituitary control]), Midbrain (vision and hearing reflexes), Hindbrain (Cerebellum [coordinates voluntary movement, posture, and balance], Pons, Medulla Oblongata [involuntary cardiac, respiratory, swallowing, and vomiting centers]); Structural unit: Neuron (Dendrite -> Cyton -> Axon -> Synapse with neurotransmitters like Acetylcholine); Reflex Arc
- Digestive System & Enzymatic Hydrolysis: Alimentary canal (Mouth -> Pharynx -> Esophagus -> Stomach -> Small Intestine [Duodenum, Jejunum, Ileum, longest segment, site of complete digestion and nutrient absorption via villi] -> Large Intestine -> Rectum); Digestive Glands: Salivary glands (Salivary amylase/ptyalin digests starch into maltose), Stomach gastric juice (HCl provides acidic pH ~1.5-2.0 and kills microbes; Pepsin digests proteins into peptones; Mucus protects stomach lining), Liver (largest gland, secretes Bile juice which has NO enzymes but emulsifies fats; stores glycogen), Pancreas (dual endocrine/exocrine gland; Trypsin digests proteins, Pancreatic Amylase digests starch, Lipase digests emulsified fats)
- Endocrine System & Hormones: Pituitary Gland ('Master Gland', secretes Growth Hormone / GH [dwarfism/gigantism], TSH, ACTH, Oxytocin [milk ejection, labor contractions], Vasopressin/ADH [water reabsorption in kidney tubules]); Thyroid Gland (secretes Thyroxine requiring Iodine; deficiency causes Goitre and Cretinism); Adrenal Glands ('Emergency glands' on top of kidneys, secrete Adrenaline / Epinephrine for 'Fight-or-Flight' response); Pancreas Islets of Langerhans (Beta cells secrete Insulin [lowers blood glucose by converting it to glycogen; deficiency causes Diabetes Mellitus], Alpha cells secrete Glucagon [raises blood glucose]); Parathyroid (PTH, regulates blood calcium)
- Excretory & Respiratory Systems: Functional unit of Kidney is Nephron (~1 million per kidney; Bowman's capsule, Glomerulus [ultrafiltration], Henle's loop, Collecting duct); Primary nitrogenous waste in humans is Urea (synthesized in liver via Ornithine cycle); Lungs (Alveoli are structural units of gas exchange; Haemoglobin carries oxygen as Oxyhaemoglobin)
- Vitamins & Deficiency Diseases: Fat-Soluble (A, D, E, K) vs Water-Soluble (B-Complex, C); Vitamin A (Retinol - Night Blindness / Xerophthalmia), Vitamin B1 (Thiamine - Beriberi), Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin - Cheilosis/glossitis), Vitamin B3 (Niacin - Pellagra), Vitamin B12 (Cyanocobalamin [contains Cobalt] - Pernicious Anemia), Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid - Scurvy, bleeding gums; destroyed by heating), Vitamin D (Calciferol - Rickets in children, Osteomalacia in adults; synthesized in skin under sunlight), Vitamin E (Tocopherol - sterility/muscle weakness), Vitamin K (Phylloquinone - impaired blood clotting)

types.name: 1. Circulatory System & Blood Components
types.desc: Cardiac cycle, heart chambers, blood cellular constituents, and ABO/Rh groups.
examples: RBCs: Lifespan ~120 days, contain iron-rich hemoglobin, destroyed in the Spleen
Blood Groups: Type O negative is Universal Donor; Type AB positive is Universal Recipient
Pacemaker: SA Node initiates normal rhythmic cardiac contractions

types.name: 2. Nervous System & Brain Anatomy
types.desc: Functional divisions of brain, voluntary control, involuntary centers, and reflex arcs.
examples: Cerebrum: Seat of consciousness, intelligence, memory, and cognitive thought
Cerebellum: Coordinates voluntary muscle movements, posture, and bodily balance
Medulla Oblongata: Controls involuntary cardiovascular and respiratory reflexes

types.name: 3. Digestive Glands & Enzymatic Catalysis
types.desc: Gastrointestinal tract organs, digestive secretions, and nutrient absorption.
examples: Liver: Largest internal organ/gland; produces bile to emulsify dietary fats
Small Intestine: Complete digestion occurs here, nutrients absorbed through villi
Stomach: Secretes HCl (pH 1.5-2.0) and pepsin for protein breakdown

types.name: 4. Endocrine Glands & Hormonal Homeostasis
types.desc: Ductless glands secreting chemical messengers directly into the bloodstream.
examples: Pituitary: Master endocrine gland controlling thyroid, adrenals, and gonads
Insulin: Secreted by Beta cells of pancreatic islets to lower blood glucose
Adrenaline: Fight-or-flight emergency hormone secreted by adrenal medulla

types.name: 5. Vitamins, Minerals & Deficiency Diseases
types.desc: Essential micronutrients, biochemical roles, and pathological deficiency states.
examples: Vitamin C (Ascorbic Acid): Prevents Scurvy; readily destroyed by cooking heat
Vitamin D (Calciferol): Sunlight vitamin preventing Rickets and Osteomalacia
Vitamin B12 (Cobalamin): Contains Cobalt; prevents Pernicious Anemia

rules.title: Universal Blood Donor vs. Recipient Rule
rules.explanation: Type O Negative ($O^-$) is the true Universal Donor because its RBCs lack A, B, and Rh surface antigens, avoiding agglutination in any recipient. Type AB Positive ($AB^+$) is the true Universal Recipient because its plasma lacks Anti-A, Anti-B, and Anti-Rh antibodies.
rules.correct: Blood group O-negative is the universal donor, and AB-positive is the universal recipient.
rules.incorrect: Blood group AB is the universal donor, and group O is the universal recipient.

rules.title: Brain Region Functional Allocation Rule
rules.explanation: Cerebrum controls intelligence, thinking, memory, and voluntary decisions. Cerebellum coordinates muscle balance, posture, and motor coordination (affected by alcohol intoxication). Medulla Oblongata controls vital involuntary autonomic reflexes (heartbeat, breathing, blood pressure). Hypothalamus controls body temperature (thermostat), hunger, thirst, and pituitary hormone release.
rules.correct: The cerebellum is responsible for maintaining body balance and coordinating voluntary motor movement.
rules.incorrect: The cerebrum is responsible for maintaining physical posture and balance.

rules.title: Bile Juice Unique Composition Rule
rules.explanation: Bile juice, synthesized continuously by the LIVER and stored/concentrated in the GALLBLADDER, contains NO DIGESTIVE ENZYMES. Its active ingredients are bile salts (sodium glycocholate and taurocholate) that emulsify large fat globules into tiny droplets for lipase action, and bile pigments (bilirubin and biliverdin).
rules.correct: Bile juice contains no enzymes but is essential for emulsifying fats in the duodenum.
rules.incorrect: Bile juice is secreted by the pancreas and contains powerful protein-digesting enzymes.

rules.title: Fat-Soluble vs. Water-Soluble Vitamins Rule
rules.explanation: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are FAT-SOLUBLE (stored in liver and adipose tissue; excess can cause hypervitaminosis). Vitamins B-Complex and C are WATER-SOLUBLE (cannot be stored in the body and must be supplied regularly in the diet; excess is excreted in urine).
words: B and C water-soluble excreted in urine
rules.correct: Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble, whereas Vitamins B and C are water-soluble.
rules.incorrect: Vitamin C is a fat-soluble vitamin stored long-term in the liver.

rules.title: Insulin vs. Glucagon Glycemic Control Rule
rules.explanation: Both are secreted by the Islets of Langerhans in the Pancreas. INSULIN (from Beta cells) LOWERS blood glucose by stimulating cellular uptake and converting excess glucose into glycogen (glycogenesis). GLUCAGON (from Alpha cells) RAISES blood glucose by breaking down glycogen into glucose (glycogenolysis).
rules.correct: Insulin lowers blood sugar by converting glucose into liver glycogen; deficiency causes Diabetes Mellitus.
rules.incorrect: Insulin raises blood glucose levels when the body is fasting.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking the heart's left ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
common_mistakes.correction: The Right Ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary artery to the lungs. The Left Ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta to the entire systemic body under high pressure.
common_mistakes.rationale: Candidates confuse the right and left sides of the heart: Right side = Deoxygenated, Left side = Oxygenated.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming Vitamin C deficiency causes Rickets.
common_mistakes.correction: Vitamin C deficiency causes Scurvy (bleeding gums, skin spots, delayed wound healing). Vitamin D deficiency causes Rickets in growing children.
common_mistakes.rationale: Associating the wrong letter vitamin with skeletal vs. connective tissue collagen disorders.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing that insulin is secreted by the liver.
common_mistakes.correction: Insulin is an endocrine peptide hormone produced exclusively by the Beta cells of the Islets of Langerhans in the Pancreas (the liver only responds to insulin by storing glycogen).
common_mistakes.rationale: Liver is the target organ for glucose storage, but pancreas is the endocrine glandular source.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing Endocrine with Exocrine glands.
common_mistakes.correction: Endocrine glands are ductless glands secreting hormones directly into the blood (e.g., thyroid, pituitary, adrenal). Exocrine glands have ducts secreting fluids onto surfaces (e.g., salivary, sweat, sebaceous glands).
common_mistakes.rationale: The presence or absence of a duct system defines the anatomical classification.

quick_revision_points: Circulatory: Human heart has 4 chambers. Normal resting blood pressure = 120/80 mmHg (systolic/diastolic, measured using a Sphygmomanometer).
Pacemaker of Heart: Sinoatrial Node (SA Node) located in right atrium. Average adult resting pulse = 72 beats/minute.
RBCs (Erythrocytes): Biconcave, lack nucleus (in humans), lifespan ~120 days. Spleen is called the 'Graveyard of RBCs'.
Blood Groups: Discovered by Karl Landsteiner. Group O is Universal Donor; Group AB is Universal Recipient.
Largest Organ of Human Body = Skin. Largest Internal Organ/Gland = Liver. Smallest Bone = Stapes (in middle ear). Longest Bone = Femur (thigh).
Human Brain: Weighs ~1.3 to 1.4 kg. Cerebrum (cognition/memory), Cerebellum (balance/posture), Medulla (involuntary centers), Hypothalamus (body thermostat).
Digestive Tract: Digestion begins in the mouth (salivary amylase). Stomach has HCl (pH ~1.5-2.0). Complete digestion and absorption occur in Small Intestine.
Pancreas: Dual gland (endocrine + exocrine). Beta cells secrete Insulin (lowers blood sugar); Alpha cells secrete Glucagon.
Thyroid Gland: Butterfly-shaped gland in neck; secretes Thyroxine containing Iodine. Deficiency causes Goitre.
Adrenal Glands: Sit atop kidneys; secrete Adrenaline (the '3F' Emergency Hormone: Fight, Flight, or Freeze).
Master Gland: Pituitary gland, situated in the sella turcica at the base of the brain, regulated by the Hypothalamus.
Excretory Unit: Nephron. Humans are ureotelic (excrete urea, produced in liver from toxic ammonia).
Vitamins: Fat-soluble (A, D, E, K); Water-soluble (B, C).
Deficiency Diseases: Vit A -> Night Blindness; Vit B1 -> Beriberi; Vit B3 -> Pellagra; Vit B12 -> Pernicious Anemia; Vit C -> Scurvy; Vit D -> Rickets; Vit K -> Bleeding diathesis.

lessons.title: Environment: Ecosystem Dynamics, Biodiversity Conservation, Climate Change, Pollution & Protocols

content_json.definition: Environmental Science and Ecology in competitive examinations (UPSC, SSC CGL/CHSL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC, State PSCs, CDS, NDA) covers ecological interactions, food chains and energy pyramids, biogeochemical nutrient cycling, biodiversity conservation regimes (In-situ vs Ex-situ), pollution chemistry (air, water, soil, e-waste), global warming, stratospheric ozone preservation, and landmark international environmental treaties and conventions.
content_json.overview:
Comprehensive Ecological Principles Framework:
- Ecosystem Architecture & Energy Flow: Biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and Abiotic components; Lindeman's 10% Law of Energy Transfer (only 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next; 90% is dissipated as metabolic heat); Ecological Pyramids (Pyramid of Energy is ALWAYS upright; Pyramid of Numbers and Biomass can be inverted in tree/aquatic ecosystems); Food Chains (Grazing vs Detritus food chains); Biomagnification / Biological Concentration (progressive accumulation of non-biodegradable toxins like DDT and Mercury up trophic levels)
- Biogeochemical Cycles: Gaseous cycles (Carbon cycle, Nitrogen cycle: Nitrogen fixation by Rhizobium/Azotobacter -> Nitrification by Nitrosomonas/Nitrobacter -> Denitrification by Pseudomonas) vs Sedimentary cycles (Phosphorus, Sulfur)
- Biodiversity & Wildlife Conservation: Levels of biodiversity (Genetic, Species, Ecological); Biodiversity Hotspots in India (Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, Sundaland; criteria: >=1500 endemic vascular plant species and >70% habitat loss); Conservation strategies: In-situ (National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves - 18 in India, Project Tiger 1973, Project Elephant 1992) vs Ex-situ (Botanical gardens, Zoological parks, Seed banks, Cryopreservation); Ramsar Convention on Wetlands (1971, Montreux Record)
- Atmospheric Pollution & Environmental Chemistry: Primary vs Secondary pollutants (Secondary: Smog, Ozone, PAN; Primary: CO, SO₂, NOₓ); Photochemical Smog (Los Angeles smog, oxidizing, requires sunlight, NOₓ and hydrocarbons) vs Classical Smog (London smog, reducing, coal smoke and SO₂); Acid Rain (pH < 5.6, caused by atmospheric SO₂ and NO₂ reacting with rain to form sulfuric and nitric acids, causing corrosion of marble / 'Marble Cancer' on Taj Mahal); Eutrophication (nutrient enrichment from agricultural fertilizer runoff causing algal blooms and biological oxygen demand / BOD spike in lakes)
- Global Environmental Treaties & Protocols: Montreal Protocol (1987, landmark treaty to phase out Ozone Depleting Substances like CFCs; World Ozone Day on Sep 16); Kyoto Protocol (1997, legally binding targets to reduce 6 greenhouse gases); Paris Agreement (COP21, 2015, legally binding goal to limit global temperature rise well below 2°C, preferably 1.5°C); Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD, Rio Earth Summit 1992); Minamata Convention (Mercury poisoning); Basel Convention (Hazardous waste transboundary movement)

types.name: 1. Ecosystem Dynamics & Trophic Energy Flow
types.desc: Energy transfer efficiency, ecological pyramids, and trophic interactions.
examples: Lindeman's 10% Law: Only 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next
Pyramid of Energy: Always strictly upright, obeying the Second Law of Thermodynamics
Biomagnification: Non-biodegradable toxins (DDT, methylmercury) accumulate maximally in apex predators

types.name: 2. In-situ vs. Ex-situ Biodiversity Conservation
types.desc: On-site habitat preservation regimes versus off-site genetic repositories.
examples: In-situ Conservation: National Parks (no human activities), Wildlife Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves
Ex-situ Conservation: Botanical Gardens, Zoological Parks, Seed Banks, Cryopreservation

types.name: 3. Atmospheric Pollution & Smog Chemistry
types.desc: Primary and secondary pollutants, industrial particulate emissions, and smog types.
examples: Photochemical Smog (Los Angeles): Oxidizing, formed by sunlight, NOₓ, and volatile organic compounds
Classical Smog (London): Reducing, formed in cool humid weather by coal smoke and sulfur dioxide

types.name: 4. Global Warming & Climate Change
types.desc: Greenhouse effect, radiative forcing gases, and atmospheric ozone depletion.
examples: Major Greenhouse Gases: Water vapor (greatest contributor), Carbon Dioxide (CO₂), Methane (CH₄), Nitrous Oxide (N₂O)
Ozone Layer: Located in the Stratosphere; depleted by Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) releasing chlorine free radicals

types.name: 5. Multilateral Environmental Treaties & Conventions
types.desc: Global treaties setting legally binding emission caps and conservation benchmarks.
examples: Montreal Protocol (1987): Protection of the stratospheric ozone layer (phases out CFCs)
Kyoto Protocol (1997) & Paris Agreement (2015): Mitigation of greenhouse gas emissions
Ramsar Convention (1971): International protection and sustainable use of wetlands

rules.title: Lindeman's 10% Ecological Energy Transfer Rule
rules.explanation: Formulated by Raymond Lindeman (1942), only approximately 10% of the energy stored as biomass in one trophic level is transferred and incorporated into the next higher trophic level. The remaining 90% is expended in respiration, growth, movement, or lost as heat. This thermodynamic inefficiency strictly limits terrestrial food chains to 4 or 5 trophic levels.
rules.correct: If primary producers generate 10,000 Joules of energy, primary consumers obtain 1,000 J, secondary consumers 100 J, and tertiary consumers 10 J.
rules.incorrect: Energy transfer increases up trophic levels, allowing apex carnivores to receive 90% of plant energy.

rules.title: Biomagnification Concentration Gradient Rule
rules.explanation: Biomagnification refers to the progressive increase in concentration of persistent, non-biodegradable, fat-soluble toxins (such as DDT or methylmercury) at each successive trophic level. Because organisms cannot metabolize or excrete the toxin, its concentration is LOWEST in primary producers and HIGHEST in top carnivores/apex predators.
rules.correct: In a contaminated aquatic food chain, the highest concentration of DDT is found in fish-eating apex predatory birds.
rules.incorrect: In biomagnification, the highest concentration of toxins is found in phytoplankton at the bottom of the food chain.

rules.title: Good Ozone vs. Bad Ozone Stratification Rule
rules.explanation: Stratospheric Ozone (~15-35 km altitude) is 'GOOD OZONE' because it absorbs harmful ultraviolet-B (UV-B) radiation, preventing skin cancer and cataracts. Tropospheric Ozone (ground level) is 'BAD OZONE' and a toxic secondary air pollutant formed by photochemical reactions, damaging lung tissues and crops.
rules.correct: Stratospheric ozone protects life on Earth from harmful solar ultraviolet radiation.
rules.incorrect: The protective ozone layer is located in the troposphere.

rules.title: Acid Rain Chemistry & Threshold Rule
rules.explanation: Normal rainwater is naturally slightly acidic (pH ~5.6) due to dissolved atmospheric $CO_2$ forming weak carbonic acid. 'Acid Rain' is strictly defined as precipitation with a pH LESS THAN 5.6, caused by anthropogenic emissions of Sulfur Dioxide ($SO_2$) and Nitrogen Oxides ($NO_x$) reacting to form Sulfuric ($H_2SO_4$) and Nitric ($HNO_3$) acids.
rules.correct: Acid rain is caused by emissions of sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, lowering rainwater pH below 5.6.
rules.incorrect: Acid rain is caused exclusively by excess atmospheric carbon dioxide.

rules.title: In-situ vs. Ex-situ Conservation Modality Rule
rules.explanation: In-situ Conservation protects species within their natural ecosystem (e.g., National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves, Sacred Groves). Ex-situ Conservation protects threatened animals/plants outside their natural habitats in human-managed facilities (e.g., Zoological Parks, Botanical Gardens, Gene Banks, Seed Banks, Cryopreservation).
rules.correct: Establishing a National Park is an in-situ conservation method, whereas a Botanical Garden is ex-situ.
rules.incorrect: A Botanical Garden is an in-situ conservation method.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking the greenhouse effect is entirely unnatural and harmful.
common_mistakes.correction: The natural greenhouse effect is essential for life on Earth; without it, Earth's average surface temperature would be a frigid -18°C rather than the hospitable +15°C. Only the enhanced, anthropogenic greenhouse effect causes dangerous global warming.
common_mistakes.rationale: Candidates conflate the baseline life-sustaining radiative blanket with runaway human-induced emissions.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing water vapor is not a greenhouse gas.
common_mistakes.correction: Water vapor is the most abundant and potent natural greenhouse gas in Earth's atmosphere, accounting for 36-70% of the natural greenhouse warming effect.
common_mistakes.rationale: Exam questions often trick candidates who believe CO₂ is the only significant greenhouse gas.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing the Montreal Protocol with the Kyoto Protocol.
common_mistakes.correction: The Montreal Protocol (1987) addresses Ozone Layer Depletion by phasing out CFCs and halons. The Kyoto Protocol (1997) addresses Global Warming by reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
common_mistakes.rationale: Both are landmark treaties from the late 20th century addressing atmospheric issues.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming human settlements are allowed inside National Parks.
common_mistakes.correction: In India, National Parks have the highest statutory protection under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972: no human habitation, grazing, or private property rights are permitted. Wildlife Sanctuaries, by contrast, permit limited traditional grazing and resource collection.
common_mistakes.rationale: Legal distinction between National Parks (strict protection) and Wildlife Sanctuaries (limited rights allowed).

quick_revision_points: Ecosystem: Term coined by A.G. Tansley (1935). Term 'Ecology' coined by Ernst Haeckel (1866).
10% Law of Energy: Raymond Lindeman (1942). Only 10% energy transfers to the next trophic level; 90% lost as metabolic heat.
Pyramid of Energy: Always upright without exception (First and Second Laws of Thermodynamics).
Biomagnification: Progressive concentration increase of non-biodegradable toxins (DDT, Mercury) up the food chain, peaking in top predators.
Ozone Layer: Located in the Stratosphere (~15-35 km). Measured in Dobson Units (DU). Depleted by CFCs producing chlorine free radicals.
Montreal Protocol: Signed on 16 September 1987 to phase out Ozone Depleting Substances (ODS). September 16 is World Ozone Day.
Greenhouse Gases: Water vapor, Carbon Dioxide (CO₂), Methane (CH₄), Nitrous Oxide (N₂O), Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), Sulfur Hexafluoride (SF₆).
Acid Rain: Precipitation with pH < 5.6 caused by atmospheric SO₂ and NOₓ forming sulfuric and nitric acids.
Eutrophication: Nutrient pollution (phosphates and nitrates) leading to algal blooms, high Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD), and fish die-offs in water bodies.
Minamata Disease: Caused by industrial Methylmercury poisoning; Itai-Itai Disease caused by Cadmium poisoning.
Biodiversity Hotspots in India: Western Ghats, Eastern Himalayas, Indo-Burma, and Sundaland.
In-situ Conservation: National Parks, Wildlife Sanctuaries, Biosphere Reserves. Ex-situ Conservation: Botanical Gardens, Zoos, Seed Banks, Cryopreservation.
Project Tiger: Launched on 1 April 1973 in Jim Corbett National Park. Project Elephant launched in 1992.
Ramsar Convention: Signed in Ramsar, Iran (1971) for wetland conservation. World Wetlands Day is celebrated on February 2.

lessons.title: Everyday Science: Scientific Principles Behind Daily Phenomena, Kitchen Chemistry & Household Physics

content_json.definition: Everyday Science in competitive examinations (UPSC, SSC CGL/CHSL Tier 1/2, RRB NTPC, State PSCs, CDS, NDA) examines the practical application of physics, chemistry, and biology in daily life. This covers everyday optical and acoustic phenomena, kitchen chemistry (pressure cookers, baking powders, curdling, refrigeration), household electronics (microwaves, LED bulbs, electric fuses), cleaning mechanisms (soaps, detergents, micelles), water purification, and common consumer materials.
content_json.overview:
Comprehensive Everyday Science Principles Framework:
- Optics & Atmospheric Phenomena: Why is the sky blue? (Rayleigh scattering: shorter blue wavelengths scatter more); Why is the sun red at sunrise and sunset? (Red light has longer wavelength, penetrates deeper atmospheric path with minimum scattering); Why do stars twinkle? (Atmospheric refraction across fluctuating air densities); Early sunrise and delayed sunset (Atmospheric refraction makes sun visible ~2 minutes before actual horizon crossing and ~2 minutes after); Mirage in deserts (Total Internal Reflection in hot air gradient); Rainbow formation (Dispersion + Refraction + Internal Reflection in raindrops); Looming (Cold atmospheric mirage in polar seas)
- Thermal Physics in the Home: Working of a Pressure Cooker (Increased pressure inside raises the boiling point of water above 100°C [up to ~120°C], cooking food substantially faster); Why does water boil at lower temperatures in the mountains? (Atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude, lowering boiling point; food takes longer to cook in open pans on hills); Refrigerator cooling mechanism (Expansion of volatile refrigerant gas like HFC-134a absorbs latent heat from the interior); Evaporative cooling (Sweating/perspiration cools the human body; water in earthen clay pots / *matka* stays cool due to evaporation through porous walls)
- Domestic Electricity & Appliances: Electric Fuse (low melting point alloy of Lead and Tin; operates on Joule heating $H = I^2Rt$; breaks circuit during overload/short-circuit); Miniature Circuit Breakers (MCBs, magnetic and bimetallic trip); Microwave Oven (Microwave radiation at ~2.45 GHz excites polar water molecules in food, causing dielectric heating through rapid dipole rotation); LED (Light Emitting Diode, electroluminescence in p-n junction, high energy efficiency) vs Incandescent filament bulbs (wastes ~90% energy as heat); Inverter air conditioners (variable frequency compressor drive)
- Kitchen & Household Chemistry: Baking Powder (mixture of Baking Soda $\text{NaHCO}_3$ and a mild edible acid like Tartaric Acid; prevents bitter sodium carbonate taste); Vinegar (4-8% dilute aqueous solution of Acetic Acid $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$); Antacids (Mild bases like Milk of Magnesia $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ or $\text{NaHCO}_3$ that neutralize gastric hyperacidity); Bleaching Powder ($\text{CaOCl}_2$, disinfectant for municipal drinking water); Rusting of Iron (forms hydrated iron oxide, causes iron articles to GAIN weight!); Ripening of fruits (Artificial ripening using Calcium Carbide $\text{CaC}_2$ which releases Acetylene gas $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2$ upon moisture contact; prohibited by FSSAI; natural ripening uses Ethylene)
- Cleansing Mechanisms & Colloid Chemistry: Soaps (Sodium/Potassium salts of long-chain fatty acids like stearic or palmitic acid) vs Synthetic Detergents (Sodium salts of alkyl benzene sulfonates); Micelle Formation (Hydrophilic ionic head faces outward into water, Hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail embeds in grease/oil dirt; agitated rinse washes away the micelle); Why soap fails in hard water (Forms insoluble scum with $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, whereas detergents do not); Milk (Oil-in-water emulsion stabilized by casein protein)

types.name: 1. Daily Optical & Atmospheric Phenomena
types.desc: Light scattering, refraction, total internal reflection, and optical illusions.
examples: Blue sky & red sunset: Rayleigh scattering of sunlight by atmospheric molecules
Twinkling of stars: Continuous refraction through shifting atmospheric layers
Early sunrise and delayed sunset: Adds ~4 minutes to the apparent length of day

types.name: 2. Thermal Physics & Kitchen Appliances
types.desc: Boiling point elevation, latent heat of vaporization, and pressure cooking.
examples: Pressure Cooker: Increased pressure raises water's boiling point to ~120°C, speeding up cooking
Earthen Pots (Matka): Evaporation of water through micro-pores cools stored water
Microwave Heating: Rapid oscillation of polar water molecules produces dielectric heat

types.name: 3. Household Electrical Safety & Lighting
types.desc: Circuit protection, low-melting fuses, and energy-efficient illumination.
examples: Electric Fuse: Lead-Tin alloy wire with low melting point to prevent circuit damage
LED Bulbs: Solid-state electroluminescence converting electricity directly into photons
Tungsten Filament: Extremely high melting point (~3422°C) used in incandescent bulbs

types.name: 4. Household Chemistry, Foods & Antacids
types.desc: Common culinary salts, acids, preservatives, and neutralization chemistry.
examples: Baking Powder: Sodium bicarbonate + tartaric acid (neutralizes alkaline bitter taste)
Vinegar: 4-8% dilute solution of acetic acid used as a culinary preservative
Milk of Magnesia: Magnesium hydroxide Mg(OH)₂ suspension used to neutralize stomach acid

types.name: 5. Soaps, Detergents & Colloid Chemistry
types.desc: Surfactants, micelle mechanics, hard water reactions, and emulsions.
examples: Soap Micelle: Hydrophobic tail traps grease; hydrophilic head dissolves in water
Synthetic Detergents: Clean effectively even in hard water containing Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺
Milk: Natural oil-in-water emulsion stabilized by casein protein

rules.title: Pressure vs. Boiling Point Altitude Rule
rules.explanation: Boiling occurs when liquid vapor pressure equals surrounding atmospheric pressure. Inside a sealed pressure cooker, trapped steam raises pressure to ~2 atmospheres, ELEVATING the boiling point of water to ~120°C, which cooks food much faster. Conversely, at high altitudes (mountains), lower atmospheric pressure DECREASES the boiling point below 100°C, meaning food takes much longer to cook in an open pot.
rules.correct: In a pressure cooker, water boils at a higher temperature (~120°C), drastically reducing cooking time.
rules.incorrect: In a pressure cooker, water boils at a lower temperature (~80°C).

rules.title: Baking Soda vs. Baking Powder Composition Rule
rules.explanation: Baking Soda is pure Sodium Bicarbonate ($NaHCO_3$). When heated alone, it releases $CO_2$ but leaves Sodium Carbonate ($Na_2CO_3$), which tastes bitter and yellowish. Baking Powder is a blended mixture of Baking Soda + a mild edible solid acid (like Tartaric Acid or Cream of Tartar). The acid neutralizes the sodium carbonate, producing pleasant tasting carbon dioxide bubbles.
rules.correct: Baking powder contains sodium bicarbonate mixed with tartaric acid to eliminate the bitter aftertaste.
rules.incorrect: Baking powder and baking soda are chemically identical single compounds.

rules.title: Soap Micelle Cleaning Action Rule
rules.explanation: Soap molecules have two ends: a hydrophobic (water-repelling) hydrocarbon tail and a hydrophilic (water-attracting) ionic carboxylate head. In water, they cluster into spherical 'micelles' where the tails dissolve in the central oily dirt/grease droplet and the ionic heads project outward into water. Agitation lifts the micellar emulsion away in the rinse water.
rules.correct: In a soap micelle, the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tail dissolves in the oil/grease droplet.
rules.incorrect: The hydrophilic ionic head of a soap molecule binds to the oily grease.

rules.title: Electric Fuse Wire Characteristics Rule
rules.explanation: An electrical safety fuse wire MUST have TWO mandatory properties: (1) HIGH RESISTANCE (so Joule heat $I^2Rt$ accumulates quickly during current surges); and (2) LOW MELTING POINT (typically made of an alloy of Lead $Pb$ and Tin $Sn$, melting at ~183°C) so that it melts and breaks the circuit before copper house wiring can overheat and ignite.
rules.correct: A fuse wire must possess high electrical resistance and a low melting point.
rules.incorrect: A fuse wire should have a very high melting point and thick copper gauge.

rules.title: Weight Change During Iron Rusting Rule
rules.explanation: When an iron nail or tool rusts, iron chemically combines with atmospheric oxygen ($O_2$) and moisture ($H_2O$) to form hydrated ferric oxide ($Fe_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O$). Because oxygen and water molecules from the air are chemically incorporated into the solid rust layer, the TOTAL WEIGHT OF THE RUSTED OBJECT INCREASES.
rules.correct: When an iron object rusts, its total weight increases due to the addition of oxygen and water mass.
rules.incorrect: When iron rusts, its total weight decreases.

common_mistakes.mistake: Thinking an iron object loses weight when it rusts.
common_mistakes.correction: Rust is chemically hydrated ferric oxide ($Fe_2O_3 \cdot xH_2O$). The mass of atmospheric oxygen and water that combines with the iron increases the total mass of the object.
common_mistakes.rationale: Candidates confuse the eventual flaking off of crumbling rust with the initial chemical synthesis that adds mass.

common_mistakes.mistake: Believing microwave ovens cook food from the inside out.
common_mistakes.correction: Microwaves penetrate food to a depth of only 2 to 4 cm from the outside. Heat penetrates deeper solely by thermal conduction from the hot outer layers inward.
common_mistakes.rationale: Popular consumer myth; microwaves do not heat from the center outward.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming water in an earthen pot cools because clay is an insulator.
common_mistakes.correction: Water cools in an earthen clay pot (*matka*) because the porous clay walls allow continuous capillary seepage of water to the exterior, where it evaporates by absorbing the latent heat of vaporization from the remaining water.
common_mistakes.rationale: Cooling is caused by the thermodynamics of evaporation, not passive insulation.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing electric fuse characteristics with heater element characteristics.
common_mistakes.correction: A fuse wire requires high resistance and a LOW melting point (to melt quickly). A heating element (Nichrome) requires high resistance and a very HIGH melting point (to glow red-hot without melting).
common_mistakes.rationale: Candidates mix up the melting point requirements for circuit breaking versus heat generation.

quick_revision_points: Sky Color: Blue sky and red sunset are caused by Rayleigh scattering (Intensity ∝ 1/λ⁴).
Twinkling of Stars & Early Sunrise: Caused by atmospheric refraction. Sunrise appears ~2 minutes earlier and sunset ~2 minutes later (day lengthened by ~4 minutes).
Pressure Cooker: Trapped steam elevates pressure, raising boiling point to ~120°C, speeding up cooking.
High Altitude: Lower atmospheric pressure lowers boiling point of water (<100°C); food takes longer to cook in open vessels on mountains.
Earthen Clay Pot: Evaporative cooling of water seeping through porous clay walls removes latent heat.
Refrigerator: Cools via cyclic expansion and evaporation of volatile refrigerants (HFC-134a) absorbing latent heat.
Microwave Oven: 2.45 GHz microwaves cause dielectric heating by rapidly flipping polar water molecules in food.
Electric Fuse: Safety device made of Lead-Tin alloy having high resistance and low melting point.
Tungsten Filament: High melting point (~3422°C) used in incandescent bulbs with argon gas.
Baking Powder: Blend of Baking Soda (NaHCO₃) and mild edible Tartaric Acid to neutralize bitter sodium carbonate taste.
Vinegar: 4-8% dilute aqueous solution of acetic acid (CH₃COOH).
Antacids: Mild bases like Milk of Magnesia (Mg(OH)₂) or NaHCO₃ used to neutralize excess stomach HCl.
Rusting of Iron: Forms hydrated iron oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O). Iron gains weight when it rusts!
Soap vs Detergent: Soaps form insoluble scum in hard water (Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺); synthetic detergents do not form scum and lather easily.
Soap Micelle: Hydrophobic tail binds to oil/grease dirt; hydrophilic ionic head faces outward into water.

previous_year_questions.question:
The following sentence has been divided into parts. One of them may contain an error. Select the part that contains the error from the given options:

'The furnitures in this historic museum showroom are extraordinarily preserved.'
previous_year_questions.explanation: Rule of Uncountable Nouns: The word 'furniture' is an uncountable noun in standard English grammar. It does not possess a plural form ('furnitures' is incorrect). Furthermore, being uncountable, it requires the singular auxiliary verb 'is'. The grammatically sound construction is: 'The furniture in this historic museum showroom is extraordinarily preserved.'
previous_year_questions.subject: English

previous_year_questions.question:
Select the grammatically correct sentence that rectifies the error in the underlined segment:

'The scissors was placed on the carpenter's workbench alongside the wooden chisels.'
options_json: The scissors were placed on the carpenter's workbench
The scissor was placed on the carpenter's workbench
A scissors were placed on the carpenter's workbench
The scissor were placed on the carpenter's workbench
previous_year_questions.correct_answer: The scissors were placed on the carpenter's workbench
previous_year_questions.explanation: Rule of Paired Nouns: 'Scissors' designates an implement comprising two connected cutting blades. It exists solely in the plural form and obligatorily takes a plural verb ('were placed'). If a singular verb is required, the phrase 'a pair of scissors was' must be utilized. Therefore, option A is the only correct sentence.

previous_year_questions.question: A, B and C enter into a partnership. A invests Rs. 25,600 and B invests Rs. 20,000. At the end of the year, out of total profit of Rs. 15,000, A receives Rs. 6,400. What was C's investment? [SSC CGL 2022 Tier 2]

previous_year_questions.question: The average of 25 numbers is 54. The average of the first 13 numbers is 52 and that of the last 13 numbers is 56. If the 13th number is excluded, what is the average of the remaining numbers? [SSC CGL 2023 Tier 1]
previous_year_questions.explanation:
Sum of all 25 numbers = 25 * 54 = 1350.
Sum of first 13 = 13 * 52 = 676.
Sum of last 13 = 13 * 56 = 728.
13th number is counted twice: 13th number = (676 + 728) - 1350 = 1404 - 1350 = 54.
If the 13th number (54) is excluded, the remaining 24 numbers have sum = 1350 - 54 = 1296.
New average = 1296 / 24 = 54.0.

previous_year_questions.question: A can complete a piece of work in 25 days and B can complete the same work in 30 days. They worked together for 5 days and then A left. In how many days will B finish the remaining work? [SSC CGL 2023 Tier 1]

Time taken by A alone = Total work / Efficiency of A = 42 / 2 = 21 days.

previous_year_questions.question: Two pipes A and B can fill a cistern in 12 hours and 15 hours respectively, while a third pipe C can empty it in 20 hours. If all three pipes are opened together, the cistern will be full in: [UPSC CDS 2023]
previous_year_questions.explanation:
LCM(12, 15, 20) = 60 units total capacity.
Inlet rate A = 60 / 12 = +5 units/hr.
Inlet rate B = 60 / 15 = +4 units/hr.
Outlet rate C = 60 / 20 = -3 units/hr.
Net rate when all open = 5 + 4 - 3 = 6 units/hr.
Time taken = 60 / 6 = 10 hours.
previous_year_questions.subject: Mathematics

previous_year_questions.question: A train 240 m long passes a pole in 24 seconds. How long will it take to pass a platform 650 m long? [SSC CGL 2023 Tier 1]
previous_year_questions.explanation:
Speed of train = Length of train / Time = 240 / 24 = 10 m/s.
Total distance to cross platform = Length of train + Length of platform = 240 + 650 = 890 m.
Time taken = 890 / 10 = 89 seconds.
previous_year_questions.subject: Mathematics

previous_year_questions.question: A man can row 6 km/h in still water. If the speed of the current is 2 km/h, it takes him 3 hours more in upstream than in downstream for the same distance. Find the distance. [SSC CGL 2022 Tier 2]
previous_year_questions.explanation:
Downstream speed D = 6 + 2 = 8 km/h.
Upstream speed U = 6 - 2 = 4 km/h.
Let distance be d.
Time difference: (d / 4) - (d / 8) = 3.
(2d - d) / 8 = 3 -> d / 8 = 3 -> d = 24 km.
previous_year_questions.subject: Mathematics

previous_year_questions.question: Two trains start at the same time from Aligarh and Delhi and proceed towards each other at 14 km/h and 21 km/h respectively. When they meet, it is found that one train has traveled 70 km more than the other. What is the distance between two stations? [UPSC CDS 2023]
previous_year_questions.explanation:
Let time of travel until meeting be t hours.
Distance by first train = 14t; Distance by second train = 21t.
Difference in distance = 21t - 14t = 7t = 70 km -> t = 10 hours.
Total distance between stations = 14t + 21t = 35t = 35 * 10 = 350 km.
previous_year_questions.subject: Mathematics

previous_year_questions.question: A sum of money amounts to Rs. 7,560 in 3 years and to Rs. 8,748 in 5 years at simple interest. Find the rate of interest. [SSC CGL 2023 Tier 1]
previous_year_questions.explanation:
SI for 2 years (5 - 3) = 8748 - 7560 = Rs. 1188.
SI for 1 year = 1188 / 2 = Rs. 594.
SI for 3 years = 3 * 594 = Rs. 1782.
Principal P = Amount after 3 years - SI for 3 years = 7560 - 1782 = Rs. 5778.
Rate R = (SI * 100) / (P * T) = (594 * 100) / (5778 * 1) = 59400 / 5778 = 10.28% approx 10.27%.
previous_year_questions.subject: Mathematics

previous_year_questions.question: A sum of money doubles itself in 7 years at simple interest. In how many years will it become 4 times of itself? [SSC CGL 2022 Tier 2]
previous_year_questions.explanation:
When sum doubles, Interest = P in 7 years.
To become 4 times itself, Interest = 3P.
Since Simple Interest is directly proportional to time:
Time = 3 * 7 = 21 years.
previous_year_questions.subject: Mathematics

previous_year_questions.question: What annual payment will discharge a debt of Rs. 6,450 due in 4 years at 5% simple interest? [UPSC CDS 2023]
